speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am honored to table in the House today the strategy entitled Sharing Our Future, the action plan that will guide Canada's Official Development Assistance (ODA) policies into the next century.
As parliamentarians are aware, the past three years have been important both for Canadian foreign policy and for the process of policy-making.
I had an opportunity to discuss that new strategy with the critics of both opposition Parties last night.
Commencing with the publication of Competitiveness and Security in 1985, a period of extensive consultation, review and reflection on the various elements and components of Canada's foreign policy in general, and aid policy in particular, has been undertaken.
Canadians and our many development partners-nongovernmental organizations and institutions, trade unions and co-operatives, the private sector, and multilateral agencies, as well as people in the developing countries-have participated in the process.
Parliamentarians, through our committees, have played an important part in giving shape to the diverse views and objectives articulated by Canadians and their organizations.
The new stragegy I am presenting is the culmination of this extensive review. And the various new policy thrusts and initiatives announced in it reflect the development vision of Canadians themselves. The strategy thus demonstrates the confidence our Government has in the wisdom, talents and commitment of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, our Government believes that a country's foreign policy must be an expression of the vision of its citizens-a reflection of their values, goals and objectives.
Our foreign policy conveys to the international community our character as a nation.

We embarked upon a thorough policy review with a firm belief in mind, a conviction, that the shaping of foreign policy and aid policy is the responsibility of all Canadians and not the exclusive domain of politicians or bureaucrats in Ottawa. The message embodied in this new Canadian strategy for a development corporation is one of which we can all be proud. Canadians care. It says much about us as a nation that Canadians accept our responsibility to be partners in building a better world, not only for our children but for all the world's children.

The strategy that will guide Canada's development assistance policies is built on three commitments I made at the beginning of my mandate: improving the delivery of our aid, fostering partnership, and reaching out to involve Canadians more fully in our development program.
My first commitment, "improving aid delivery", reflects the belief of many Canadians that we need stronger aid policies which are relevant and appropriate, both to those we seek to help and to Canadians as well. Better program delivery will mean that the right Canadian resources reach those most in need, when they need our help the most.
The second, "fostering partnership", captures the spirit of commitment that Canadians showed in their strong response to the crisis in Africa three years ago. It reflects our desire to build on the consensus achieved at that time. Canadians want

March 3, 1988
Statements by Ministers
to create new partnerships-both domestically and internationally-so that together we can build a better world.
And my pledge on reaching out to the public responds to the desire I sense among Canadians to learn more about development, to be better informed-so they can take part more fully.
Before 1 highlight some of the new policy directions we are announcing today, let me quickly sketch for you the principles that will guide our initiatives in international development.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, in responding to the Report of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade (SCEAIT) last September, the Government endorsed the committee's proposal for an ODA charter.
The charter has four pillars: The primary purpose of our development effort is to help the world's poorest countries and people.

Canada's aid policies must strengthen the human and institutional capacity of developing countries to solve their own problems in harmony with their natural environment.

In setting objectives for development assistance, developmental priorities must prevail.

We must strengthen the links between Canadian citizens and institutions, and those in the Third World. In short, partnership.
[ Translation]
With these principles as the foundation of our policy, our priorities to help focus our projects and programs are: alleviate poverty; design structural adjustment policies that take into account their human impact on the people they are designed to assist; strengthen our emphasis on the role of women in development;

-foster environmentally sound and ecologically sustainable programming; strive for food security; and emphasize energy availability.

The four pillars, complemented by the priorities I have mentioned, constitute the charter for Canada's development assistance program.
Beyond this, we are announcing a significant number of new programs and initiatives in our strategy. Here are some of the highlights:
We have created a "new eligibility framework" for our ODA-one that provides flexibility so we can achieve the goals
to which we are committed, including: eradicating global poverty, concentrating on the poorest countries and people, and ensuring that our aid policies are more focused and more relevant.

The new framework makes it easier to take into account the human rights performance of various countries when deciding upon the nature and scope of our assistance efforts.
[ Translation]
We have also decided to divide the aid program into two distinct parts-each having half of the ODA budget.
The first part, called the "Partnership Program", will be for initiatives and programs shaped by our Canadian and international partners in development.

The second will support Canada's national initiatives program of bilateral assistance and other contributions to development carried out mainly on a government-to-govern-ment basis.

Mr. Speaker, to improve "program delivery", significant numbers of aid personnel will be decentralized both to existing overseas posts and to four new regional field offices.

These field offices, one for the countries of the Southern African Development Co-ordination Conference, the second for the Sahel, a third in the Caribbean and another for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, will help to ensure that future CIDA initiatives are better tailored to local needs and circumstances. Higher levels of approval authority will be delegated to field personnel.
[ Translation]
To ensure that our programs encourage self-reliance rather than dependence, "human resource development" will become the lens through which all our efforts will be viewed. Creating indigenous capacity to enable each country to solve its own development problems will be our steady focus.
To achieve this, many initiatives are put forward-including one to double the number of CIDA-sponsored students and trainees, both in Canada and the Third World.

New guidelines to govern our food aid policies and to consider the ecological and environmental impact of our aid efforts are also important elements of the strategy.

These measures, and others we are announcing, are designed to improve the effectiveness, relevance and quality of what we do in the Third World.
March 3, 1988

To strengthen our commitment to partnership-one of the four pillars of our aid strategy-new initiatives are being launched to enhance the participation of our development partners from the private sector, non-governmental organizations and training institutions.

For the private sector, the budget of CIDA's Industrial Cooperation Program will be doubled and its parameters enhanced. General lines of credit will be established in up to 20 countries and guidelines governing their use will be made more flexible.
[ Translation]
Measures to encourage co-operation between Canadian universities and training institutes and those in the Third World are being announced today. Universities will be invited to prepare proposals for centres of excellence in development studies.
Canada's non-governmental organizations and institutions are among the world's leaders in international development. To enhance their contribution, numerous initiatives are proposed in the strategy-along with an increase in the amount of ODA allocated to supporting their efforts.

The various agencies and institutions that make up the multilateral system provide some of the most precious and effective tools for promoting international development and cooperation.

The World Bank, the United Nations Children's Fund, the World Health Organization, the World Food Program, the United Nations Environment Program, the Commonwealth and la Francophonie are but a few examples of the diversity of agencies and programs the multilateral system offers for the effort to achieve global progress.
Mr. Speaker, Canada remains committed to a strong and vital multilateral system, and we will continue to strive for renewal and revitalization.

To facilitate access to the aid program by Canadians and raise levels of public awareness of development issues, I am announcing today an extensive multi-faceted public education and outreach strategy.

This strategy is designed both to enhance CIDA'S presence in Canada's regions and to increase public awareness of the challenges and opportunities of international development.
Mr. Speaker, these are a few highlights of our new strategy for ODA-a strategy formulated by Canadians for building a better world.
International development is vitally important to the future of our interdependent world.
Statements by Ministers
Repression, epidemics, famine, desertification and ecological degradation are both the symptoms and the causes of poverty and underdevelopment.

Too often in the past, aid-giving has been considered exclusively a moral or humanitarian issue, haves helping have-nots. We must change that perception. Aid must be regarded not just as charity but as an investment in our shared future.

Mr. Speaker, only through the eradication of global poverty can we create an environment that nurtures the tremendous creative potential of the human race, and frees it to build the better world we all want to see.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, very often it is the task of a critic to try to find fault with what has been presented in a Minister's statement, and certainly I will try to be loyal to that responsibility. There are some matters of great concern to the Liberal Party and as the critic for the Liberal Party on human rights and international development I would like to bring these to the attention of the Government and the Canadian people.
It is also the responsibility of a critic to commend the Government when it does take positive action. The Government has taken a number of very important, solid steps forward. I want to commend the Minister for the thoroughness of her statement in reply to the report made by the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade entitled For Whose Benefit. That report was made after a year of study, consultation, and travel. The Minister has taken to heart many of the important issues which were brought up.
For example, she has reported today that the Government now intends to, first, emphasize aid to the poorest nations. She has also pointed out that human resource development will now take a front line role, an important priority. She pointed out that decentralization in the field, which the committee recommended, will take place. This means that the people most affected will have a direct input into what is happening in their country and will be partners in what takes place. She has pointed out that there will be a reduction in the amount of tied aid, especially for weaker and poorer countries. That, too, is a positive development. She has pointed out that there will be a much expanded student scholarship program and aid in education.
There are a number of other items on which she reported. We should all take heart from this and be pleased. I want to indicate the satisfaction of my Party and myself with these promised programs of action by the Government to follow the recommendations which we made in the all-Party standing

March 3, 1988
Statements by Ministers
committee which made a unanimous report entitled For Whose Benefit on what we thought should be done. I wanted to make those positive points at the outset.
While I realize that the Government has accepted a number of our recommendations, I do have a concern that there is an unwillingness by the Government to establish concrete and sound criteria for the examination of human rights violations in countries which receive our official development assistance and to determine what amounts of money we should be giving.
In the committee's report, which we hoped would be taken to heart by the Government, we recommended that as part of over-all Canadian foreign policy we apply a universal, consistent, and transparent manner in the way in which we assess human rights violations and make our grants.
Further, we recommended the development of a classification grid for recipient countries which would provide incentives for good behaviour as well as penalties for poor human rights performance. We made that recommendation because we were dissatisfied with the way in which the Government has been handling the granting of official development assistance to countries where there are human rights offences and violations and where Governments have been despotic.
We further recommended an annual ODA human rights review to be tabled in Parliament and referred to the Standing Committee on Eluman Rights. That was a serious effort to try to deal with a most serious area of concern, and the Government has not addressed itself to this other than with a promise that human rights will be reviewed by Cabinet. We are now told that Cabinet will judge the human rights record of receiving countries and determine the "appropriate channels for Canadian ODA and bilateral allocations for each country". Mr. Speaker, can you imagine Cabinet undertaking that responsibility? I myself cannot see Cabinet sitting in session assessing each nation.
We must seriously ask what the Government really means when it says that the Cabinet will be looking into this. Who is the Cabinet? Will it really be some faceless bureaucrats who will make recommendations? Will it be the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), or will it be some claque of Neanderthal, red-neck Tory back-benchers holding up aid or development assistance because they do not like the political stripe of some recipient Government? Or will we perhaps have no guidelines at all, as has been the case until now, and continue to muddle around with no clear line of procedure as to how we will link our concern about human rights to the way in which we grant aid to other nations?
This is an area of real concern to us and I hope that the Government will realize that the Canadian people will not accept this program as a reply to what Canadians across the country were telling our committee was an outstanding concern of Canadian people, that being how we assess the human rights performance of other countries and how we link our policies in some fair, objective way that will allow us to give grants to countries which are, to some degree at least, respectful of human rights, and to withhold aid from countries that are grossly violating human rights and our bilateral
assistance. It must also raise the question of how we will deal with our multilateral grants.
The greatest concern that we on this side of the House have about this reply by the Minister is that it misses the most fundamental concern of all. The most fundamental issue before us today is the amount of aid this country is going to give. We were promised that at some point in the future the figure would be .7 per cent of GNP. In fact, during the last election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised that Canada's ODA funding would reach .7 per cent of the Gross National Product by 1990. We have to ask what has happened to that promise.
At present our ODA is only at .5 per cent, not .7 per cent. It is going to be maintained at .5 per cent until 1991 and will gradually be increased to .6 per cent by 1995 and .7 per cent of GNP by the year 2000. That means that the promise which was made is completely broken. We are going to stay where we are. We are not going to reach .7 per cent by 1990. The Government is now talking about .7 per cent of gross national product by the year 2000. That is the bottom line.
The question is, what is the priority of the Government? Is it to buy nuclear submarines to patrol the Arctic Ocean to see where other nuclear submarines are and make note of it? Is that how we are going to spend our funds when we know perfectly well that much of the world's peace is at stake because of the unstable and tragic economic problems in other nations? Or are we going to carry out our traditional policy as Canadians of trying to carry a strong Overseas Development Assistance Program which will bring peace and stability to nations throughout the world?
The inability of the Government to deal with the most fundamental issue, that is, to provide the funds that are necessary for overseas official development assistance, is the critical issue which we wish to criticize. It is broken promises. By 1990 another $1 billion was supposed to be injected into this effort. Instead of increasing the amount of aid in order to keep that promise, the Government is saying that we will stay as we are, that we will not increase anything, and that there will be no effort for some time to come.
Therefore, while the program has some assets which I have noted in terms of the priorities of where our funds are going and the way in which they will be spent, there is no serious effort to live up to our promises and obligations and to reach the goals which this country has set for itself. The Government is once again failing to put its money and itself where its mouth is.

subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to respond to the Minister's statement on behalf of the New Democratic Party. I would like to thank the Minister for her courtesy in making a copy of her statement available to me and my Liberal colleague last evening. It helps to facilitate the business of the House and a friendly spirit on the floor of the House when that sort of courtesy is extended.
March 3, 1988

When we consider development assistance, perhaps we should begin with the recognition that Canadians are fundamentally a generous people. I presume that this is true of other peoples in the world as well.
When we hear of other people who are in trouble, whether through earthquakes, drought, floods or war, we want to be able to help where we can. CIDA is the Government tool for generosity. It provides emergency assistance in all of these and other emergencies.
We need to go beyond spontaneous generosity which fades with yesterday's television news. We need a national policy commitment to assist in the development of other nations.
For the past number of years we have had that national policy commitment through CIDA, recognizing that development assistance is not just a matter of generosity but a recognition that we live in one world and that our peace and security and our children's peace and security really depend upon the development of a decent standard of living for all men and women, boys and girls in this world. This was underlined by the title of the Brundtland report presented to the United Nations a year ago, Our Common Future. The report tabled in the House today builds on that theme and is entitled Sharing our Future.
We share a future with all the peoples of the world. We cannot have a fortress Canada or fortress North America that ignores the needs and the rightful aspirations of other people for a decent standard of living and human rights.
I want to commend the Government for the review that has taken place of foreign policy and development assistance policy over the last two years. It was a privilege for me to be able to work on both the Special Joint Committee on Canada's International Relations and to work on the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade when it did its review on development assistance.
One of the highlights of both those committees was the degree of public interest in external affairs and in development assistance. This kind of public support is absolutely essential and we must build on it.
One of the recommendations of our report was that there should be a development charter. We said that this development charter should be clearly enshrined in legislation that would be clear and binding. Today the Minister tabled her report and talked about a development charter, but the charter will not be enshrined in legislation. To that extent it is a weak charter because there is nothing binding in it. It is simply words that have been tabled in the House of Commons and that have no more binding force than any other words spoken in this Chamber.
The committee recommended very extensive decentralization. I am pleased that an important first step toward decentralization is being taken in this report. It is important to
Statements by Ministers
recognize that the contract awarding authority remains in the Ottawa-Hull region. I think that should be decentralized as well, which would have the effect of encouraging large and small companies that are interested in development to maintain a consistent presence in the developing countries where they wanted to work. When the final contracts are awarded in the Ottawa-Hull area, it leaves it open to people who are able to have an effective lobby in Ottawa. I am not sure this that is the direction we want to take.
I am pleased that the Government is accepting the emphasis on human resource development. Over the last number of years there has been an increasing recognition of the importance of women in development and the need for their participation to be built in at all levels. This is something that needs to be monitored. We give recognition to that in our reports and it is something that is recognized in policy. It must also be consistently monitored to ensure that it is being followed through. The same is true for the growing recognition of the need to have environmental concerns built into our development assistance.
I am pleased with the Minister's announcement about a doubling of scholarships. I believe education is key in the whole development process. One concern I have relates to the public participation program. A couple of years ago there were many concerns that the public participation program budget might be slashed. My concern, as I look at what the report says, is that the entire program could be turned into a public relations program for CIDA. Throughout the country we have a number of learner centres that have had an arm's length relationship with CIDA which occasionally have been very critical of what Canada has been able to do in terms of development assistance. Indeed, representatives of a number of these learner centres appeared before our committees, and I believe they made some fairly trenchant critiques of what CIDA was doing.
It states in the report that there will be a consultation with these learner centres to assess their potential for taking on responsibilities relating to distributing films, publications and so on. I am not opposed to that, and perhaps that is a useful function, but I am concerned that that consultation should not be used as a way of bringing these learner centres into a form of control by CIDA so that they really become extensions of the public relations department.
1 am pleased to see the reduction of tied aid from 80 per cent to 50 per cent for the sub-Sahelan area, and to 66-2/3 per cent for other areas. I believe this is a good first step.
Like my Liberal colleague, 1 am concerned about the Government's failure to take adequate action on the whole area of human rights. This was one of the fundamental areas of concern of Canadians as they appeared before our committee. They wanted to be sure that the aid moneys that are being

March 3, 1988
Petitions
disbursed by Canada are being used in a proper way and not going to repressive regimes.
My Liberal colleague outlined what the committee recommended, a very open process that would involve a public review by the House of Commons standing committee. Instead, there is a cabinet decision. The open process is necessary because there are situations such as the one now where the Government has renewed assistance to Guatemala. I want to read briefly what the 1987 annual report of the Inter-Church Committee on Human Rights in Latin America, says about Guatemala. It states:
Summary executions and disappearances are still a daily occurrence. Neither the government's claim that this violence is the result of common delinquency nor its attempts to reduce it through heavy investments in new police equipment adequately responds to the challenge. It is scandalous to treat these hundreds of violations of the right to life as of relatively minor concern simply because numbers are no longer in the thousands as they were a few years ago.
Along with its inability to put an end to current human rights violations, the present Guatemalan government has shown itself unwilling or incapable of initiating even a preliminary investigation into the fate of past victims of such abuses.
And it continues. The problem is that while that kind of knowledge about Guatemala has been available, the Government, last November, just prior to the visit of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to Central America, used that visit as the occasion for announcing resumption of aid to Guatemala. People across Canada who are concerned about development assistance wonder how development can take place in a climate of repression such as we have in Guatemala.
The same is true of El Salvador. The Inter-Church Committee stated:
Human rights problems of a gross, systematic and continuous nature continued in El Salvador during 1987.
It talks about arrest and detention with little meaningful legal protection. It continues:
Such practices represent a general government policy aimed at stifling popular dissent.
Death squad activity continued and indeed appeared to be increasing as the year drew to a close. The brutal October assassination of a prominent human rights activist thrust the survival of such practices back into the consciousness of the international community.
Undoubtedly the impunity with which past human rights offences have been treated in El Salvador and the Government's attempt to reduce the struggle for human rights to a propaganda battle have done little to contribute to the creation of a better human rights climate.
The Council on Hemispheric Affairs in the United States, in its eleventh annual report, singled out El Salvador and Chile as being among the worst violators of human rights in Latin America last year. Yet when I wrote to the Minister last fall, sending a copy of a report which had been produced by a teacher from my constituency who had visited El Salvador, which documented human rights violations in El Salvador, the Minister replied:
Setting aside for the moment differing views of the human rights situation in El Salvador, there is a broad agreement in this country that Canadian aid should be used to benefit those in greatest need. This is certainly true in the case of our program in El Salvador.
It is not just a matter of differing views of the human rights situation in El Salvador. It is a fact that the Government refuses to recognize that the human rights situation in El Salvador is abominable and disgraceful. We cannot make excuses and say that we hope it will be all right.
The same is true for the scandal of human rights in East Timor,and we have a massive aid program for Indonesia. I commend the Government for some of the steps it has taken. I regret that the aid levels are still below the target that was promised by the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he appeared before the United Nations just after he was appointed to his office. I remind the Liberals that they also cut back on the level of development assistance when they were in government.
I look forward to the implementation of this program. I understand that the standing committee is going to have the Minister come before it. We will review the way in which this program will be administered. I urge the Minister and CIDA to get on with this. I also asked them to try to bring forward a clearer public policy to link human rights and development assistance. Development assistance simply cannot take place in a climate of repression.

subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO TRANSPORT OF PLUTONIUM OVER NORTHERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour today to present two petitions on different issues. They are both certified correct pursuant to Standing Order 106. The first petition is from a number of citizens of the Northwest Territories. The petition indicates a concern that the United States and Japan have proposed to fly plutonium over the Canadian North, representing devastating consequences to both the Canadian environment and its people in the event of an accident or act of terrorism.
The petitioners say that Canada has not been consulted by either the United States or Japan, which effectively challenges Canadian sovereignty in our North. They feel that allowing such flights over Canada would be contributing to nuclear proliferation, something to which Canada should be completely opposed. Therefore, they call upon Parliament to recognize the dangers of such flights and to say a very strong no to the transport of plutonium over northern Canadian territory.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FREE TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present another petition signed by citizens
March 3, 1988

of Swift Current, Saskatchewan, as well as other centres, who indicate that they believe the federal Government lacks a mandate from the people of Canada to conclude a free trade agreement with the United States. They also believe that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised in the course of the trade discussions that Canadian sovereignty would not be compromised and feel that Canada's sovereignty has been compromised.
The petition goes on to state a number of other issues which 1 will not raise because I will be filing this petition. However, fundamentally the petitioners call upon Parliament to dissolve now and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to either accept or reject the proposed trade deal with the United States during a national general election.

subsubtopic: PORNOGRAPHY-SUPPORT FOR BILL C-54
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and duty to present a number of petitions on behalf of residents of southwestern Saskatchewan concerning Bill C-54. The petitioners indicate their concern that pressures exerted by various permissive minority groups may cause Parliament to water down and weaken this legislation. The petitioners therefore humbly pray and call upon Parliament to support the Bill which will make it illegal to manufacture, import, sell or rent pornographic material as defined in the Bill.
They call upon Parliament to pass the legislation without dilution in the belief that it gives recognition to the inherent dignity of individuals, particularly women and young people who are most vulnerable to exploitation in this area.
1 have in fact 23 petitions from residents of Swift Current, Burstali, Leader, Frontier, Eastend, Fox Valley, Simmie, Herbert, Cabri, Ponteix, Maple Creek, Sceptre, Mendham, Prelate, Admiral, and Hazlet, Saskatchewan, containing over 1,600 signatures, all relating to the same issue.

subsubtopic: PROHIBITION OF DISCRIMINATION ON BASIS OF SEXUAL ORIENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the privilege to present a petition, which is signed by a substantial number of constituents of my riding and residents from different areas of Ottawa who note that in October of 1985 the subcommittee on Equality Rights of the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General of this House, submitted a report to the House recommending that the Canadian Human Rights Act be amended to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in all areas of federal jurisdiction.
They further note that in March, 1986, just two years ago today, the Government accepted this report and its recommendations and said it would take whatever measures are necessary to ensure that sexual orientation is a prohibited ground of discrimination.
The petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to ensure that the Government acts to implement that recommendation and that commitment. I have the privilege of submitting their petition and I hope that it moves the Government to act.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FREE TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the privilege and responsibility to table a petition signed by residents of Toronto, Capreol, Barrie, Hornepayne in the Province of Ontario, as well as Chatham, Merlin, London and Kingsville, also in Ontario. These petitioners point out that in fact the Government had no mandate to conclude a free trade agreement with the United States.
They also point out that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had promised in the course of the negotiations with the United States that Canadian sovereignty would not be compromised. They also point out that this proposed free trade agreement not only denies Canadians the secure access to the U.S. market, which was the key objective in these negotiations, but in fact it threatens the loss of hundreds of thousands of Canadian jobs.
The petitioners call upon Parliament to allow the people of this country to decide on this very important issue by a dissolution of Parliament and the calling of a general election by this Government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too have a petition to present which conforms with Standing Order 106. It deals with the subject of the trade deal with the United States and is signed by residents of the City of Toronto.
In the petition the residents of the city indicate their view that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised in the course of bilateral trade negotiations that Canadian sovereignty would not be compromised, yet the trade agreement negotiated by the Government threatens to remove the very fabric of Canadian political and economic sovereignty by removing the power of the Canadian Government to effectively control foreign ownership, to develop Canadian energy resources in the best interest of Canadians and to equalize opportunities between regions.
Therefore they conclude that there must be an election called to endorse or to reject this trade deal before it is accepted.

subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO SALES TAX ON FOOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a number of petitions signed by petitioners from Richard's Landing and Hilton Beach. On the petition are several dozen names of constituents of mine who are calling on the Government not to impose a sales tax on food.
They point out the large number of regressive taxes which have been imposed already on dental supplies, snack food, candies and soft drinks, all of which are close to food. They know that the documents of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that were tabled in the House stated that food should not be taxed, but they did not say that food would not be taxed. That is the real concern of these constituents.
I hope the House will take this matter into consideration, especially the Minister of Finance, who I know wants to do something good for the country. I am sure that he will be well impressed by this petition.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
That this House notes that the flow-through share tax provision has been instrumental in revitalizing mining communities and regions across Canada, and consequently urges that the initial benefit level of this provision not be reduced but be retained to encourage mineral exploration and development by small and medium-sized companies.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this debate concerns the question of the Government's decision to terminate the flow-through share provisions which have encouraged an extraordinary amount of development in northern Quebec, northern Ontario, western communities, Nova Scotia, and even in Schefferville, the ghost town left by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he was the President of the Iron Ore Company of Canada which has seen some $19 million worth of investment in exploration because of the flow-through share provisions that have been in force since 1983.
March 3, 1988

This specific motion will be voted upon when we will be able to see how some Conservative Members of Parliament, who I know are very unhappy about the Minister of Finance's (Mr. Wilson) decision, will vote on this particular measure. It urges that the initial benefit level of the flow-through share provision not be reduced but be retained to encourage mineral exploration and development by small and medium-sized companies.
Last year the Prime Minister declared that we are in the process of building two Canadas, one which is rich and promising and one which is underdeveloped and underemployed. He was right.
What we are really talking about is a very important measure which has had enormous consequences in terms of providing growth and development on a self-sustaining basis in mining areas and in frontier areas across Canada. This is the Auto Pact of the mining sector of Canada. Perhaps the Government is trying to gut the Auto Pact under the trade arrangement with the United States as well. We reject that. We reject this measure which denies continuation of activity to regions which have benefited enormously. We believe that if this measure is maintained, it can be focused in such a way that it can be confined to junior mining companies which carry out the bulk of mining exploration and development. This can be done in ways which would permit a broader range of the population to participate rather than being confined to higher-income Canadians as the major providers of mining investment.
The White Paper on Tax Reform last July proposed cutting the earned depletion allowance, which is an essential part of the flow-through share mechanism, from 33 per cent, which is where it stood before Christmas, to 16.33 per cent in July of 1988, and to zero per cent in July of 1989. The finance committee suggested that the 33 per cent rate be maintained for a year and then be cut to 16 per cent to the end of 1989. We did not concur with that recommendation. But even that recommendation was not accepted by the Government. The Finance Minister's sole concession has been to extend the 16 per cent rate so that it will last for 18 months from July of this year until the end of 1989.
During the course of the discussion on the question of flowthrough shares, New Democrats have been criticized. It has been suggested that we have adopted contradictory positions. That is not true. During the 1984 election campaign my Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), was critical about the fact that we have various substantial amounts of tax expenditures and of tax benefits for corporations in Canada. The total of tax expenditures in Canada amounts to something in the order of $25 billion of $30 billion a year, according to the Auditor General. Little or nothing of that amount has in fact been attacked or really taken head-on by the Government.
What we made clear in the 1984 election campaign was not that these tax concessions should be wiped out automatically
Supply
but that they should be evaluated. Those that were demonstrably of benefit should be maintained, just as those that were demonstrably not of benefit and merely cost the taxpayer should in fact be reduced or eliminated.
Earlier this week we met with representatives from across the country in the save flow-through share committee. They brought their campaign to save the flow-through share regime to Ottawa on Monday and Tuesday of this week. From the side of the New Democratic Party, which is consistent, we indicated that we thought the program should be focused on the mining regions and on the junior mining companies. The people from the industry accept and agree with that position. They are not saying that the regime, which was put in by the Liberals in 1983 and which was overly generous to the large mining companies, should be maintained per se. They are not saying that a system which largely benefits taxpayers earning over $200,000 a year should be maintained per se. They are saying that the perceived benefits in their regions should be maintained for the junior mining companies. That is what we are asking Members on all sides to support in this votable motion here today. What is unusual is not the New Democratic Party's position, but that the Conservatives are withdrawing the flow-through program and not putting anything in its place.
Since this issue first emerged in the House of Commons in a high profile manner in December of 1986, I took the trouble to look at our discussions on this issue as a consequence of the 1986 Budget. At that time the Government proposed a modest enrichment of the flow-through share program that existed at that time. On behalf of my Party, I was critical of a further enrichment. I say now, and I said then, that it should be targeted.
At that time I made it clear that rather than voting against that particular motion, measure, or clause in the tax Bill, "We could have tried to change, amend and improve the various measures being put forward by the Government". I went on to
say:
I decided, and my colleagues accepted, that where you have a measure which should fundamentally be re-thought, which is far too broad for the declared purpose, which is to get some needed exploration expense and activity going in the northern parts of my province, that is, Quebec, the oil and gas, areas and so on, rather than simply saying there is a bit of good here and there is a lot of bad, we should simply tell the Government to stop it, take the measure away, start all over again, and strike out the loopholes. Then, if the Government has to have targeted measures in the form of tax credits, grants or other means to encourage certain types of desirable activity, for goodness' sake let it do it that way, but let it not do it in the broad brush kind of way-
That was being proposed at that time. That makes sense. That is consistent. I said, "let us evaluate it". We had not done an evaluation at that time. Let us focus it in order to ensure that we were not making unnecessary commitments of tax resources and that we were getting what we wanted for the desirable activity which is to get needed exploration expense and activity going in the northern parts of my province, in Quebec, and in the rest of the country.

March 3, 1988
Supply
It is interesting that at that time the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) responded with a paean of praise for flow-through shares. He stated:
I think the Hon. Member knows that flow-through shares and the tax arrangements for them are not designed for the riding of Ottawa Centre. They are designed ... for northern Ontario, northern Quebec, the Northwest Territories, the Yukon, and northern Manitoba, Alberta and so on.
As a matter of fact, it is the northern parts of our provinces that are the most neglected parts of our society economically and in every other sense. We must do something for those parts. That is what is behind the flow-through shares.
The Minister of State for Finance went on to say:
-quite frankly, flow-through shares have been very effective in creating very meaningful economic activity in a neglected area of Canada... This policy-is aimed at helping the people in northern Canada and making sure that risk decisions are not taken by Government but by the private sector.
I am in the uncomfortable position of agreeing with the Minister of State for Finance. What is curious is that only six months after that fulsome praise for flow-through shares, the Government turned around and scrapped its support for flowthrough shares. The Government is the one that did the flip-flop. The Government is the Party that changed its mind, not the New Democratic Party.
In responding to concerns which we and many other people have raised about the flow-through shares, in December, in its response to the finance committee, the Government acknowledged that there was widespread concern about the impact of flow-through share financing. Then the Government said that all it would offer would be temporary assistance, in the event that there were depressed prices or economic downturns affecting exploration activity in Canada. In other words, after the mining communities go back to 25 per cent unemployment, then the Government might do something.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, this week, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) stated before the save flow-through shares committee, and I quote:
I cannot approve of measures aimed at shielding the mining exploration sector from market forces, nor do 1 support tax measures that reward activity without considering results.
So market forces must prevail. And the Minister also said, and I quote:
These changesin the flow-through shares program
-are part of the overall tax reformand the Minister is not prepared to make any changes at all. [English]
He has cut loose the mining communities despite the evidence of the impact of this particular tax measure, which I maintain meets the New Democratic Party's criterion, that is, it is clear that the benefits have been very substantial, and it is possible to have those benefits at a cost which is reasonable and justifiable in terms of what this does for regional development.
Of course, the Government does not understand very much about regional development. It has consistently cut spending on regional development since coming to office in 1984. This particular measure that the Government inherited from the Liberals has encouraged $2 billion worth of mining exploration activity in Canada. The indications we have from studies financed by the prospectors in Quebec and by the Government of Quebec indicate that the mines already opened under this program have generated an estimated $1.5 billion of production per annum, some 66,000 jobs, $2.8 billion worth of added value, and additional taxes for the federal Government in Quebec of some $300 million per annum after deducting the cost of the tax incentives.
The Quebec Prospectors' Association told the finance committee, "To abandon this program would signify the elimination pure and simple of junior companies which produced almost all the mining discoveries between 1980 and 1985".
[ Translation]
The results have been fantastic, Mr. Speaker. In Abitibi, about $500 million was spent on exploration during the past three years, and 15,000 jobs were created. This has promoted small business. In three years, unemployment dropped from 28 per cent to 5 or 6 per cent in the Abitibi area, saving a lot of money in unemployment insurance benefits and welfare payments.
In Schefferville, $19 million was spent in a community that had been closed down by the former president of Iron Ore Canada, the present Prime Minister of this country.
In Murdochville, in the Gaspe, another region with one of the highest unemployment rates in this country, $6 million was spent.
In Thetford Mines, where 350 new lay-offs were announced in the asbestos industry, two Quebec companies are opening up two chromium deposits, and $20 million will have been spent in 1987 in this region.
We see the same thing happening at La Fosse in Labrador and Ungava. Some 800,000 square kilometres have been staked for exploration purposes by a number of companies, mostly junior companies headed by Quebecers, and these are young entrepreneurs and companies based in the area, not in Montreal or Toronto.

With this program we are seeing the development of an authentic, new mining industry based in these regions. It is genuine regional development, rather than the boom-bust pattern of mining development in which large mining companies situated in Toronto, Montreal, or abroad turned the exploration up when they felt like it and then turned it down flat.
March 3, 1988

We have seen a rate of mine openings and findings such as we have never seen in the country before. There has been an increase from three or four mines being opened per year over the last 30 years to about 15 mines being opened per year. Last year alone some 34 mines were opened across Canada, mainly in the gold mining sector and largely because of this particular program. These mines are generating jobs, every one of them. They are generating tax revenue. They are helping our balance of payments. They are creating regional development for regions which had just about given up hope of anything else happening for them.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the Association des prospecteurs du Quebec, which wants the flow-through shares program to be maintained, is supported in that province by the unions, the Montreal Stock Exchange, the Quebec Chamber of Commerce, our own Party and the Parti Quebecois, by over a dozen municipalities who are affected by this measure, by the James Bay Development Corporation, and I could go on, but my speaking time is limited.

Support for this program is not confined to Quebec. In Nova Scotia, not renowned as a mining province, it is estimated that $100 million was invested in mine exploration and development in 1987, mainly on the eastern shore of Nova Scotia where we know that unemployment has been particularly high. Just in the small community of Sheet Harbour, with 2,500 people, in the riding of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay), the Eastern Shore Development Commission estimates expenditures of $100,000 per week. That is real regional development.
In Kirkland Lake, Ontario, which has suffered economic decline for a half century, from the boom of the 1920s, there has been $70 million in mining exploration and development over the last three years. However, we now have the first casualty. Northfield and Queenston Gold Mines cancelled a $50 million mining development program in that area as soon as the Minister of Finance confirmed that flow-through provisions were coming to an end. In fact, after July of this year we are told that no further equity financing will be raised under this particular program because all the juice has gone out of it as a result of the Minister's statement.
If we look at Red Lake, in the riding of the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry), we see that unemployment has dropped from 20 per cent to 6 per cent. There are 45 drills working there, whereas there were three or four drills working just four years ago.
Uranium City was dying, yet it has now been revived because of exploration based upon flow-through shares.
I want to make clear that I have been consistent in terms of pressing the Minister. I offered him suggestions in a letter of last December, which specifically called for flow-through shares to be targeted to small companies that do not have other
Supply
forms of income against which they can write off their exploration expenses. We have also suggested the possibility of there being tax credits allowing smaller income earners to take advantage of the particular program rather than confining the benefits to people who are at or near the top rate of income tax. The Minister of Finance has simply said: "No".
In conclusion, I know how my colleagues from the ridings of Churchill, Kamloops-Shuswap, the Yukon, Skeena, Nickel Belt, Kenora-Rainy River, Thunder Bay-Atikokan, and Thunder Bay-Nipigon will vote on the particular measure. We in the New Democratic Party will vote for these benefits to continue because of the value they have brought to mining communities and for them to be focused on smaller junior mining companies that can take the greatest advantage of them.
I want to know where the Minister of National Revenue stands on this particular question. How will the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil) vote? Will he vote with the Government or for his constituents? How will the Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) and the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) vote? How will the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain), who we know is uncomfortable with this particular provision, vote, or the Hon. Member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley (Mr. McCuish)? How about the Hon. Member for Abitibi (Mr. St. Julien) who was so strong in criticizing me in 1986 and then spoke so strongly for flow-through shares? Will he be consistent, or will he flip-flop with the Minister of Finance on the particular issue, when unemployment has dropped from 25 per cent to 6 per cent in his area because of the particular program?

Is the Hon. Member for Abitibi (Mr. St-Julien) going to vote against the interests of his constituents and in favour of the Minister of Finance, or will he vote for his constituents and for regional development in the Abitibi area?

How about the Hon. Member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Desjardins)? We know his private views. Does he have the courage to stand and say publicly that the New Democratic Party is right in putting forward this motion and that the Minister of Finance is wrong in withdrawing exploration and development from mining communities across Canada?
I believe that these questions must be answered by government Members. May they live with their conscience if they vote with the Minister of Finance or if they just abstain today, because taking a walk means that they are supporting the Minister of Finance.
Finally, because my time is up, I want to say that this question will not die in the House of Commons today. This question is very lively in mining communities across Canada. The people in those communities are looking to where the

March 3, 1988
Supply
various Parties stand right now. They understand the position of the New Democratic Party. They do not understand what the Government is doing in pulling the rug from under mining communities so that it can cut the taxes on people earning over $100,000 per year. This is what the Government wants to do, it seems to me, or perhaps it is so that it can cosy up to the Americans over the trade deal and say that it is not supposedly subsidizing that particular sector.
The Conservatives will be on the line in the election campaign-did they stand up for mining communities or did they ignore the plight of mining communities which will be adversely affected by the withdrawal of this particular measure?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member is aware that the benefits of flow-through share financing, particularly depletion, go to those Canadians who are upper income investors, people who earn $60,000, $70,000, $80,000, and more. I find it difficult to understand why the Hon. Member is saying that he wants to extend depletion, because then he is encouraging this type of investor to pay little or no tax, something against which he and his colleagues have been railing, and on which we have taken some action.
Could the Hon. Member explain why-and I share his concern about the position of mining communities right now, and 1 will address it in my remarks-why the New Democratic Party is proposing the extension of depletion or the continuation of depletion, which is a subsidy that benefits upper income Canadians and helps them to pay little or no tax? Could he explain that to the House?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am sorry that the Minister seems to ignore constructive suggestions that were made to him, particularly in the letter that I wrote on December 16, 1987, in which I made a number of suggestions.
I said that the measure should be focused on small, nontaxable companies, that is, junior mining companies. Also I said:
-the Government should offer a tax credit or its equivalent to small investors who wish to participate in financing Canadian mineral exploration and development. This would give individuals a tax saving for relatively small investment-and make the incentive proportional to the mining expenditure rather than the taxpayer's income. As a consequence, new investment may come from those communities in which mining takes place and not just from high-income taxpayers who currently purchase close to one-half of the dollar value of flow-through share issues.
In arguing that the benefit should be maintained for junior mining companies, it is quite clear that we proposed that there should be substantial changes in the program.
What appalls and really bothers me is that the Government could, in six months, go from having the Minister of State- and I assume he speaks with the same authority as the Minister of Finance-say that flow-through shares have been effective in creating very meaningful economic activity in a neglected area of Canada, to taking the opposite position and
deciding that they will totally neglect mining areas by withdrawing flow-through shares over a short period of time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member misses the point here. There will be a continuation of the level of activity of about half of what was done in 1987 without any change in what we have proceeded with right now in income tax reform. The Hon. Member is saying we should extend the earned depletion, something which would clearly help those Canadians who are in the high-income brackets and large, multinational companies. Again, the Hon. Member is talking out of both sides of his mouth. Members of the New Democratic Party are saying that they would stop that dead in its tracks.
How is it that the Hon. Member can say that we should improve the attractiveness of flow-through share financing if he does not want it to spill over into allowing high-income Canadians not to pay taxes? He does not understand the nature of the flow-through share provision and the impact of the depletion on the flow-through share financing. We cannot limit it to investors who are working in Val d'Or or Temis-camingue. Anyone can buy these. What we have done in tax reform is to reduce the attractiveness of them. We admit that that is true, but that was a clear objective of tax reform in order to avoid what the Hon. Member has been saying for many, many years, which is that we have tax provisions which help high-income Canadians pay no taxes. The Hon. Member is talking out of both sides of his mouth and he does not understand which side he is talking out of when he opens it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if anyone is being hypocritical and if any Government is talking out of both sides of its mouth, it is the Conservative Government which is in power in Canada right now. I quote the Minister of State for Finance who said on December 16, 1986, as recorded in Hansard at page 2171:
As a matter of fact, it is the northern parts of our provinces that are the most neglected parts of our society economically and in every other sense. We must do something for those parts. That is what is behind the flow-through shares.
That is what the Minister's colleague, the junior Minister of Finance, had to say just 15 months ago. Now the Minister of Finance is saying: "Gee, we cannot do this". If that is not hypocritical, I do not know what is.
Since he has not looked at the letter, I would remind the Minister of my letter to him of December 16 in which I said:
However, I believe we can alter the nature of the flow-through share mechanism to prevent abuses while retaining the real economic benefits that emerge from it as an incentive to mining activity.
Firstly, flow-through shares could be directed to small, non-taxable companies of a specific size as they are in the oil and gas sector. At present, too many large, profitable corporations take advantage of flow-through shares at great cost to the federal treasury.
Since it is junior companies that engage in high-risk, grass roots exploration, it is those companies that should chiefly benefit from this measure.
March 3, 1988

The Minister says that it is impossible to target the benefits in that particular way. We talked with representatives of the affected communities and of the junior mining companies who were in Ottawa earlier this week. They do not see any problem with targeting the measure in that way. There is not a problem with targeting it in the oil and gas sector and there is no reason why that cannot be done in the mining sector as well.
The real issue that the Minister ignores is the fact that this program has brought enormous economic benefits to communities from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Those communities are having the rug pulled out from underneath them and this Government does not give a damn.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has not indicated by his decision a bit of a cosy relationship with large multinational mining companies as opposed to small, junior companies. A bonanza sale will soon occur and has already begun. The small exploration and mining companies have, as a result of flow-through share issues, been exploring and developing in the country. As they have made their claims and explored and developed their properties, they have identified good ore prospects. Now they will be unable to hold those prospects and develop them further because of a lack of equity financing.
I feel that the Minister of Finance knows this. That means that these properties will now go onto the market because the companies will be desperate for funds. They will need to sell off these properties, and who will buy them if not the large, multinational mining companies?
I would ask my hon. friend whether or not he feels that it is the case that the Minister of Finance has cosied up to the large mining companies and will now exploit the situation of junior companies being forced to sell their properties at fire-sale prices.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think there is a very real risk in precisely that area. I return to the basic facts which are astonishing. Last year, 34 new mines opened across Canada. The rate of mine finding in Canada has risen from 3 or 4 per year to 15 or 16 per year in the course of the last 3 or 4 years. That is an extraordinary accomplishment. This is not the kind of possibly inflationary growth that occurs within 50 miles of the Finance Minister's riding in Toronto. This is growth in regions of the country where there are resources waiting to be summoned into action.
Before the junior mining companies were able to secure financing through flow-through shares, large robber baron corporations did much of the exploration and development for as long as short-term profits could be made. When returns were diminishing or there was an economic downturn, these corporations closed down operations completely and left the regions devastated.
The cyclical boom and bust of the resource sector has always plagued mining communities, and the flow-through share program has helped these mining communities break
Supply
their reliance on non-resident businesses by encouraging junior mining companies resident in the areas that contribute directly to other economic spin-offs to projects. If, as my hon. friend for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) has indicated, the consequence now is that they are forced to sell out to the multinationals, we will basically be going back in history. That is a sorry and unfortunate tale of boom and bust which I think the mining communities want to and should be allowed to avoid.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated in my question to the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), I am very pleased to be involved in this debate. It gives me a chance to state where the Government stands on the important Canadian mining industry.
This industry is very important to the Canadian economy and particularly to the northern regions of Canada. We have seen over the early 1980s, through a period of good management, cost reductions and a good amount of reinvestment. The Canadian mining industry has become one of the most efficient in the world. Today, the industry is stronger and more resilient than it has been in its existence, and that is due to the hard work done by the Canadian mining companies, the miners and the communities themselves. It is paying off.
In 1987, the mineral industry was remarkably vigorous. According to recent government estimates, Canadian mineral production jumped by 17.5 per cent last year to $16 billion, with gold production up more than 32 per cent alone. This level of exploration activity reached record levels in 1987 and it is an achievement that is not likely to repeat itself this year, regardless of any changes in the tax provisions relating to flowthrough shares.
We as a Government are committed to keeping this industry strong, growing and able to respond to the opportunities in the world market-place. Because of this commitment, the Government retained its tax reform initiatives, a system that is highly advantageous to the mining industry. Under tax reform proposals, we have ensured that companies pay no income tax at all until all capital costs of a new mine or major expansions have been fully recovered. With tax reform, companies' preproduction development expenses can be claimed as incurred. With reform, we have provided a very generous resource allowance so that companies will be able to invest, prosper and create permanent, long-term jobs for Canadians.
The mining industry, therefore, continues to benefit greatly from highly advantageous tax treatment compared to most other sectors of the Canadian economy and compared to our competitors abroad. In fact, the mining industry has the lowest marginal tax rate of all industrial sectors. This favourable tax treatment ensures that new mines can be brought rapidly into production, creating thousands of new jobs in regions which historically have been hardpressed. These are permanent jobs

March 3, 1988
Supply
that will continue for the life of the mine, not just simply during the drilling season.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, we strongly support regional development. This is why on December 22 my colleague Robert de Cotret announced a series of consultations which will pave the way for new programs designed to meet the needs of Quebec's peripheral regions. These consultations with regional spokesmen are now under way with a view to focusing on their priorities. What we want is a diversified economy.
[English)
As well, we have given the people of northern Ontario new tools to develop and diversify their economy through the FEDNOR program. Again, my colleague from Sault Ste. Marie is involving the local communities in better targeting this assistance.
Our commitment to the mining industry is also evident in the fact that we retained a tax system that fully recognizes the special risks involved in the exploration for and development of new mines. Under tax reform we have provided companies with a 100 per cent write-off for all their exploration costs. Contrary to misconceptions generated by Members opposite, particularly the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre, we have not terminated flow-through shares. We have retained the flowthrough share mechanism which allows companies to pass their unused tax benefits on to investors. This mechanism is available only to the mining and oil and gas industries.
These special provisions, when combined with the $500,000 lifetime capital gains exemption and the special favourable treatment of exploration expenses under the investment loss rules, provide investors with strong incentives to put equity investment into mining companies.
We improved the provision in December following consultations with the industry so that it recognizes some of the problems that developed last year as a result of the problems in Canadian stock markets. These provisions are of particular benefit to junior mining companies which are critical to a vigorous, competitive mining sector.
The exploration incentives contained in our tax system are the strongest incentives offered to any industrial sector in Canada. No other sector can lay claim to a better system. [Translation]
Under the tax reform companies will be allowed to write off 100 per cent of their exploration expenditures. Contrary to the erroneous allegations made by Members opposite, we have retained the flow-through share mechanism so that companies will be able to pass their unused tax benefits on to their investors. This mechanism is available only to oil, gas and mining companies. These special provisions, coupled with the $100,000 lifetime capital gains tax exemption and the special preferred treatment of exploration expenses under the regulations governing investment losses, are a strong incentive for investors interested in the mining sector.
These provisions are particularly beneficial to junior mining companies which are the very foundation of a vigourously and competitively expanding mining industry. Our tax system features exploration incentives the likes of which are unavailable in any other industrial sector in Canada. No other sector can claim to be better treated.
[ English]
It is a true economic incentive to encourage productive investment. I stress the words "economic incentive" because one of the primary objectives of tax reform is to ensure that business and investment decisions are made on the basis of strong economic merit rather than on tax shelter merit.
A corner-stone of the tax reform measures we have proposed is a system of lower personal and corporate tax rates. Instead of a host of loopholes available to a select group of companies and individuals, we propose to provide the best economic incentive of all, and that is lower tax rates. We have got rid of loopholes in the system introduced by previous Governments and so roundly condemned by the NDP. These loopholes permitted high-income taxpayers to pay little or no tax at the expense of ordinary Canadians. We have also got rid of the tax shelters which the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre has so often criticized in this House. However, we have retained the very important flow-through share provision as a true incentive, even though the Hon. Member argued as recently as last December that we should have got rid of it.
To reduce our personal and corporate tax rates we must broaden the tax base. This includes our planned phase-out of earned depletion which currently allows an investor to write off $133 for every $100 invested in mining exploration. In other words, we are eliminating a direct subsidy in the tax system. This is so because earned depletion provides a deduction in excess of the actual amount spent by companies on exploration and development. This is consistent with the thrust of the greater fairness and equity that we are implementing in tax reform.
Investors in mining exploration who take advantage of flowthrough shares will also continue to enjoy advantages in capital gains since only 50 per cent of exploration expenses will be included in their investment loss account, thus improving their access to the lifetime capital gains exemption.
In the past several months the financial markets have changed quite markedly. As a result of the severe stock market downturn last October, the mining industry, indeed all industries, face an uncertain investment climate. There have been numerous signs of difficulty ahead for the mining industry. Virtually no equity issues have been completed since October 19. The two major issues attempted by the market have encountered significant difficulties. Share prices across the board are down. Mining shares have dropped even further. The prices of gold and silver recently softened, while investors have fled from equity issues. In fact, the riskier the equity, the faster the flight.
March 3, 1988

The point I am underlining here is that it is far more the problems in the capital markets than it is in the tax system which have affected the market for flow-through shares. It is clear that investors, big and small, have adopted a wait-and-see attitude towards putting their money into any equity. It is also evident that investors are looking for less risky investments such as the bond markets and have decided to postpone their investments in mineral exploration and other forms of risk investment at least for the time being.
Thus, despite one of the most favourable tax regimes in the world for mining, there continues to exist a great concern in the mining regions of Canada that tax reform is killing flowthrough share financing, and with it the exploration activity it finances. As I said, this is simply not true.
First, flow-through shares are not the only source of funds for exploration. The vigorous financial rebound which the mining industry enjoyed means that it is now better able to finance its own exploration activity internally. Cash flow has increased from $320 million in the first quarter of this year alone to more than $1 billion. I am confident that a good portion of this increased cash flow will find its way into funding exploration and development of new mines.
Earlier I said that exploration this year was not forecast to repeat the record rate of 1987. Let us look at the reasons why. In 1986, a very healthy year for the industry, exploration spending was $650 million. In 1987 it almost doubled to $1.2 billion. Clearly that level is not sustainable. If Members opposite talked to the industry as we have done they would know that the industry itself believes exploration was overheated and that 1988 could not, indeed should not, be a repeat of the year before.
In 1987 there was a confluence of events which artificially boosted spending. First, there was the strong bull market in stock markets until October. Second, mineral prices rebounded from recent lows. Finally, the tax incentives themselves prompted high-income investors to buy a record number of flow-through shares. These investors were not miners. They were not local entrepreneurs. They were high-income individuals who were taking advantage of an overly generous tax incentive to mine the federal Treasury. The tax structure was inappropriate. The industry knew this. We knew it. We acted to change it. We acted to change it as was recommended by the NDP Member for Ottawa Centre talking out of one side of his mouth. As the system overheats, the potential for abuse increases dramatically. The scarcity of special equipment and skilled workers results in greatly inflated drilling charges. Inefficient exploration is undertaken late in the tax year.
As Minister of Finance this entire situation gives me and the Government a great deal of concern, as it should Members opposite. In the aftermath of the crash of October 19, we do not want to see the mining industry transformed from an
Supply
overheated situation to a frozen one. We want to see a healthy mining exploration industry in Canada, but we also want an industry that is driven more by market forces than by tax incentives. No industry, indeed no region, can isolate itself from changing patterns in the international market-place.
That is why I said in June and reiterated in December that temporary measures during periods of economic downturns or depressed equity prices may be necessary to ensure the survival of exploration activities in Canada. This is why I have instructed my officials to meet with the various segments of the industry and assess this market situation in light of the current stock market softness and weakening prices for precious metals. If further measures are needed, they will be measures aimed at encouraging investors, particularly in smaller mining companies, and not tax shelters as my friend from the New Democratic Party seems to want.
As I have said, the Government remains committed to the mining industry. Our tax reform proposals with our lower tax rates will provide the ultimate incentive for investors, the ability to keep more of what they have earned. We promised to monitor the situation closely and we will. We will be looking carefully at the levels of exploration activity taking place to determine what, if any, action is warranted.
I will close by making some remarks on what I see as blatant political opportunism by both the Liberal and the New Democratic Parties. Let us not be fooled by the rhetoric of the Liberal Party. They have said that they would restore flowthrough shares. We have not taken away flow-through shares. The two key changes which reduce the attractiveness of flowthrough share financing as an investment are some tightening in the capital gains rules and in depletion. We have left some exemption for capital gains, but the Right Hon. Leader of the Liberal Party (Mr. Turner) said he would scrap all of the capital gains exemption. That in itself would be a far bigger hit on flow-through share financing than anything we have proposed in tax reform.
As I said, depletion is a subsidy, mainly to big companies to pay for the lower personal income tax rates for the average Canadian. Is the Leader of the Liberal Party going to put that back? What would then happen to the lower personal income tax rates which are going to be brought about for the average Canadian through tax reform?
The New Democratic Party said that it was going to stick to its principles. Gerald Caplan is quoted as saying:
I think that the Party would be making a mistake if it publicly repudiated
decades-long policy at this stage-
