speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on the motion before the House today, dealing with flow-through shares.
Before starting my speech, perhaps I may provide some background for the debate and explain exactly what a flowthrough share is. Sometimes I think that Members who do not represent mining areas, or Canadians who are following the debate at home, must wonder whether we are talking about some strange creature from another planet which for some reason is of particular interest to people who live in mining regions and remote areas. A flow-through share is a tool for financing mining exploration, developed a number of years ago to promote exploration in remote areas of this country and thus assist regional development.
Earlier, I heard the Minister say it was a very generous tax measure. I do not quite agree with his interpretation. Suppose we compare a furniture manufacturer with a mining company. A company that manufactures furniture and spends $25,000 or $30,000 or $40,000 or $50,000 to find new markets in New York, Chicago, Vancouver or wherever, can deduct those expenses from its profits, because the money is invested in the company's future. The same applies to the mining sector. A mining company spends money on exploration to guarantee the future of the company, like the furniture manufacturer who was looking for new markets. Both the cost of exploring markets and the cost of exploring new resources in order to continue mining operations may be deducted from profits.
March 3, 1988
Flow-through shares make it possible for a company that is not expected to make a profit within the next few years to pass the profits on directly to the shareholder. Instead of doing so five or ten years later when the profits come in, it is done right away, and the company pays taxes later on. That is where I disagree with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) who says that the program in its amended form is very worthwhile. It does not do any more for operations as risky as mining exploration than it does for any company that spends money on exploring markets.
Mr. Speaker, that being said, I must say I am rather astonished at the attitude taken by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy).
The day before yesterday, I went to see the "Save Flowthrough Share" committee, and there were about 300 people present from all over Canada. I told these people on Tuesday that tomorrow, on the Opposition day for the Liberals, I would table in the House a motion on flow-through shares, asking the Government specifically to maintain the earned depletion allowance of 33 1/3 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, how surprised I was yesterday when I realized that for the past year and a half, the Socialist Members of the NDP had fought not only against flow-through shares, but even against the very principle of tax incentives. Not only are they retreating, making an about turn of 180 degrees, of 360 degrees, not only are they changing their position, but they have the gall to move in the House a motion urging the Government to maintain the 33 1/3 per cent of the earned depletion allowance on flow-through shares.
I am sure that the mining industry as a whole and those associated with it will not be fooled by this trick of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) and will realize just how opportunistic the NDP can get in this debate.
Mr. Speaker, I have emphasized for over 18 months the need for flow-through shares and the principle of tax incentive as tools for regional development in Canada. I believe I was the only one at first, and I felt I was preaching in the desert. The mining industry would never have believed that a Tory Government would abolish the earned depletion allowance on flow-through shares and completely killed the program. The general public and also the regions which are not aware of the benefits resulting from earned depletion allowance on flowthrough shares paid only minimal attention to this debate.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party's position on this issue is well known. I explained it in the House in 1986, after the NDP Member for Ottawa Centre had moved an amendment to a tax legislation aimed at completely eliminating flow-through shares.
At the time, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre said this,...
March 3, 1988



It was on December 16, 1986, that the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre tabled a motion to amend the Income Tax Act. Had it been adopted, the amendment would have resulted in the elimination of the flow-through share mechanism. The main reason the New Democratic Party wanted to eliminate the flow-through share mechanism was that it was used mainly by wealthy Canadians. That is pure NDP policy. If you are wealthy, you are a bad Canadian.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre talked about flowthrough shares as a tax loophole, a tax avoidance mechanism. To my surprise last night and this morning I read that the same Member was tabling a motion to reintroduce the earned depletion after having said what he said in December, 1986. That is political expediency, for sure.
The position of the Liberal Party is well known. I explained our policy in my speech answering the amendment proposed by the NDP to abolish flow-through shares. This is what I said:

Speaking in French in the House on December 16, 1986, Mr. Speaker, I made the following comment, as reported on page 2171 of the House of Commons Debates'.
Mr. Speaker, I have trouble understanding the reasoning behind the motions presented by the Members of the New Democratic Party. When the Liberal Government introduced these measures, as a stimulus to economic development in the mining areas of Quebec and Northern Ontario, the results were extremely positive.
Mr. Speaker, 1 added a little further on that investments were made as a result of the flow-through share tax incentive and that by so doing, the Liberal Party of Canada had come up in favour of regional development. We said also that the tax system could and should be used as a tool of regional development and that, in this sense, tax incentive should be maintained. What we felt was wrong was not the tax incentive itself, but the abuses it could lead to in some regions of this country.
Mr. Speaker, this is why I shall repeat later on what I said in reply to the Minister of Finance's Budget speech in 1986 and what I said on other occasions in this House and in the minority report in support of the concept of regional development and of the need for the Canadian Government to have a truly national regional development policy and to have the ability to use the tax system as a privileged instrument.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, when Phase I of the tax reform was being considered in committee, the Liberal Party objected to the proposal of the Minister of Finance. Our opposition was reflected in the minority report tabled in the House in November, 1987, in which we clearly recommended that the 33 1/3 per cent earned depletion allowance on flow-through shares be maintained. This recommendation can be found on pages 18 and 19 of our minority report and was our recommendation No. 11 for the tax reform. We recommend that flow-through shares be maintained.
Why, Mr. Speaker? For many reasons related to regional development, job creation and the competitiveness of the Canadian mining industry throughout the world.
Supply
The main reason the Liberal Party recommended that the flow-through share mechanism be maintained is not only because it helped to create thousands of jobs in the regions or because it helped to raise more than $2 billion but because it represents an innovative way of establishing harmonious collaboration between the Government and the private sector. Let me elaborate a little bit on that subject.
First, it created jobs. Employment in our regions has increased substantially because of the earned depletion on flow-through shares. The Minister is dead wrong when he suggests that we in the Liberal Party are trying to give a false indication. I have repeated time and time again that what we are talking about here is the 33 per cent earned depletion allowance because it is a risky business and because exploration went down the drain in 1982 and 1983. This is why we introduced the measure. It was to help the remote areas of the country that can live only through their natural resources. We created that program to help the regions to develop and to help the mining industry which has no profit, no expectation of profit, to find a way to go ahead with exploration. It creates jobs.
In Val d'Or and Rouyn, for example, where the rate of unemployment was 28 per cent, it is now down to 6 per cent. The Minister of Finance may claim that he had something to do with that. The only reason that this thing happened is because of the 33 per cent earned depletion on flow-through shares. It is a risky business. This is why we think that the earned depletion allowance should remain. It is a risky business because when one spends thousands and thousands of dollars to dig a hole in the soil thinking that one may find some copper, gold or silver one never knows until the money has been spent. It is a very risky business. This is why I say that without the 33 per cent earned depletion allowance the mechanism of flow-through shares cannot work and will not work.
The Minister talked about the stock market crash. He said that following the crash not only has the mining industry not been able to raise equity but all other sectors have not been able to raise money. This is an additional reason why the Minister should keep the earned depletion allowance of 33 1/3 per cent in place. It is because of the difficulties that the whole industry will have in raising money. It is not the time to cut the program to a level at which the program will not be workable. It is not the time to cut the benefits of the program when other factors are playing against the mining industry, particularly exploration.
We think that earned depletion and flow-through shares should remain because they are good mechanisms to have the public sector, the Government and the private sector work very closely together. It is of direct help to junior exploration companies. Without direct involvement of the Government only the big multinational companies will have the profit and the cash flow to carry out exploration.

March 3, 1988
Supply
Another reason that the earned depletion allowance should be kept, and I have been saying this for 18 months, is because of its regional development implications. The flow-through share mechanism is part of a future Liberal Government's strategy for regional development. It has been in the past and it should remain in the future.
It must be remembered that the total economic and regional development envelope has been reduced by the Tory Government by close to $2 billion since it took power. Not only has it cut direct grants for regional development but it is now killing the flow-through share mechanism by eliminating the earned depletion allowance.

Mr. Speaker, if we want to know about the regional impact, we can look at a study carried out by the accounting firm of Maheu-Noiseux in co-operation with engineers for the Association des prospecteurs du Quebec. This study was funded in part by the Quebec Government. I would like to refer to some of the recommendations contained in this study of approximately 150 pages, which deals with all aspects of the mining industry, especially in Quebec and northern Quebec.
This study indicates that, in Quebec alone, there has been a net creation of 50,000 jobs a year. This figure is in person-years. There is an added value of $2.1 billion. Tax revenue generated in 1985 amounted to $400 million and the cost in taxes to $239 million. In other words, tax incentives cost the Government $239 million and tax revenue as a result of the economic activity generated by the industry amounted to $400 million. This is why I do not understand the attitude of the Minister of Finance. He says that he wants to protect Government revenues. However, the study shows that, in Quebec alone, this program has produced additional tax revenues of $160 million because of the economic activity generated by the industry and the fact that the welfare benefits and unemployment insurance which used to be paid to people in these regions were replaced by positive action and new jobs.

I said that the flow-through shares with the earned depletion mechanism of 33 per cent is a way to have good collaboration between the private sector and the Government. It is my profound belief that the private sector is and must remain the driving force of economic growth in the country. But it is also my belief that the Government has a role to play in the development of the economy.
This role is to create an environment, and in the case of flow-through shares, a fiscal environment, favourable to the emergence of private initiatives. The kind of co-operation that is taking place between the Government and the private sector in the case of flow-through shares is to some extent the
practical way of co-operation. It is simple. It is done without any direct involvement of the Government in the production process itself. It is done without any heavy Government bureaucratic overhead. It is done by helping private corporations gain better access to capital. It is done by reducing the risks incurred by investors in the mining exploration corporations. Quite obviously, it is done in favour of the economic development of the remote areas of the country where there are so many vulnerable one-company towns.

The Liberal Party believes that the kind of co-operation that now exists between the private sector and the public sector, in the case of flow-through shares for resources and especially in the mining industry, is vastly superior to any system of direct government subsidies. Direct subsidies often involve a lot of red tape, become discriminatory and stifle the companies one wants to help. Flow-through shares, with the earned depletion allowance of 33 1/3 per cent, not only preclude this red tape, they are an essential tool of the Government's regional development policy.
Now that the Conservative Government is cutting back on funding for regional development, it wants the regions to develop themselves, using their own resources. And now the Government is removing the main program that was helping the mining industry in these regions.

I wanted to raise another issue which, in my view, has been overlooked in this debate. It is the impact of the trade agreement with the United States and the future use of tax incentives.
According to many people, including the respected firm of Clarkson Gordon, Woods Gordon, it is not sure at all that the Government will be able to introduce new tax incentives in the future without inducing some kind of retaliation by the United States. The following is a direct quote from the newsletter of Clarkson Gordon, Woods Gordon:
Although the existing tax incentives will be grandfathered according to the Agreement, it is important for all Canadian business people to recognize that expanding the list of such incentives could induce a responsive trade action by the U.S.
Yesterday the Minister stated that this was not a serious study. If we cannot believe the words of Clarkson Gordon in the areas of accounting, business activity, and economic development, I wonder on whom we should rely for good expertise.
You have indicated to me, Mr. Speaker, that I have only a few minutes left.
March 3, 1988

Unfortunately, 1 will not have enough time, but I hope to have another opportunity to explain what we think should be done to prevent abuse of the system.
Mr. Speaker, before I finish, I would like to move an amendment to the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy). I think his motion is too vague, and if the Hon. Member was sincere about what he said, I imagine he will accept this amendment. I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster):
That the motion be amended by adding after the second "that" the words:
"because of the 33 1/3 per cent earned depletion allowance".
and adding after the second "provision" the words:
"and, specifically, the 33 1/3 per cent earned depletion allowance".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party's policy on tax incentives has been discussed on at least two occasions here in the House. I said at the time that to prevent abuse, we should have what I called a tax incentive box that would work along the same lines as a registered retirement savings plan. You could put in a certain amount of money annually or a certain percentage of your income, and the incentive would help achieve regional development objectives or perhaps develop our cultural industries, such as the film industry. However, Canadians would not be able to use these tax shelters to avoid paying income tax. Everyone would pay income tax, and I also said that the tax incentive box could be used instead of the minimum tax. In fact, it would be much easier to get rid of the minimum tax introduced by the Conservatives, a tax that does not achieve what it is suppose to achieve because first of all, it is complex, and if you pay minimum tax one year, you still have seven years to get it back. Anyone who is not completely devoid of intelligence and imagination should be able to manage his affairs in such a way that he can recover the minimum tax he paid within seven years' time. That was our proposal for stopping abuse of the system.
As for the time frame, I said in the House and I said to the representatives of various mining organizations that we believe each tax incentive should have an automatic five-year expiry date that will oblige Parliament to review the measure, not necessarily in order to abolish it but to see whether the intended objective was met. If it was not, the incentive could either be repealed or amended and improved.
As for changes in the earned depletion allowance of 33 1/3 per cent that is being reduced to 16 1/3 per cent and eventually to zero, there should be no problem in 1988, because it is still in fact, and as far as the companies are concerned, especially big corporations like CNP and NIM, the decision on share issues for 1988 was made in 1987. So there should be a certain amount of activity.
However, in addition to the earned depletion allowance that will disappear by 1989, there are also the Minister's proposed changes in taxing capital gains.
We know that until quite recently, only 50 per cent of capital gains were taxable. According to the Minister's proposals, however, 75 per cent of capital gains will now be taxed at the marginal tax rate. Since flow-through shares are deemed to cost zero cents because their purchase cost was deducted from the investor's income for the previous year, when the shares are sold, the full selling price is considered a capital gain, which is then taxed at 75 per cent instead of 50 per cent.
So when you add the reduction to zero of the earned depletion allowance-33 1/3 per cent to 16 2/3 per cent to zero in 1989-to the capital gains tax which takes a greater share, you realize that the risk is too great. You would be better advised to invest your SI00 in some other type of less risky activities.
People are wrong when they say it's a tax evasion, for it is a sort of reverse RRSP. When we invest money in an RRSP, what do we do? Instead of paying the income tax in the current year, we postpone paying it until our retirement and we start paying income tax at the then marginal rate when we retire.
In the case of flow-through shares, it is the opposite. We offer the tax advantages immediately at the time of the investment, and that is the reason why we refer to it as earned depletion. Which is called "epuisement gagne" in French. We offer the tax advantages immediately at the moment of investment, instead of offering it at the time the company which is making profits may start deducting its expenses from its profits. This does not cost a cent to the Government, except that instead of paying in three, four or five years, we pay now, which makes it possible for people to carry out mining exploration when they want.
This also makes it possible for junior companies not only to get involved in exploration, but to keep and develop these mines, something which was practically impossible before because of the required cash flow. But now it is possible.
March 3, 1988

That is why I say that the Tory Government's action today will turn off the tap for mining exploration and prevent junior companies from maintaining their involvement both in mining exploration and development.

Mr. Speaker, Pope John Paul II recently received in audience participants in a study conference on the right to life. I would like to put on record some of his remarks. He said:
Unconditional respect for the right to life of the conceived but unborn human person is one of the pillars sustaining every civil society. When a state places its institutions at the disposal of those who may act to suppress the life of the unborn child, it renounces one of its primary duties and its own dignity as a state.
A state has as its primary duty the defense of the fundamental rights of the human person especially of those who are weakest. And who is weaker than an unborn child?

The legalization of abortion has been inserted as a foreign body bearing within itself the seeds of corruption.
How is it still possible to speak of the dignity of every human person when the killing of the weakest and most innocent is permitted?
The state must always reflect as that of being a place where a person, every person is affirmed in his comparable dignity.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have an opportunity to participate in today's debate sponsored by the New Democratic Party. It is appropriate to remind Members what we are debating today. The motion is as follows:
That this House notes that the flow-through share tax provision has been instrumental in revitalizing mining communities and regions across Canada, and consequently urges that the initial benefit level of this provision not be reduced but be retained to encourage mineral exploration and development by small and medium-sized companies.
Without going into the details of the flow-through tax mechanism suffice it to say that this mechanism is recognized by miners, those living in mining communities, and those serving the mining industry in all parts of Canada, as being one of the very few tax expenditure programs that makes sense.
I know I do not have to remind you, Mr. Speaker, but perhaps it would be worth-while reminding some others, that some time ago the New Democratic Party conducted what it called Tax Probe '86. One of the recommendations offered by Tax Probe is that the Government ensure that corporate tax expenditures aimed at investment and job creation be overhauled to make sure that the tax benefits conferred are gained
only on the basis of demonstrated performance. Flow-through shares are an example of a tax incentive that has, in the main, worked. This motion recognizes that that particular tax program has resulted in considerable benefits accruing to Canadians, particularly in the regions of Canada. This motion is an effort to improve the nature of those flow-through shares by targeting them more closely to the small and medium-sized companies that are almost by definition 100 per cent Canadian-owned.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext: What was that report?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
My friend, the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), asks, "What was that report?" Tax Probe '86 is a report on the tax system prepared by the New Democratic Party. It identified this particular provision as one of the tax provisions that makes a great deal of sense, particularly when one considers the development and exploration activity that has occurred in places like northern British Columbia, which is one of the highest mineralized zones in all of Canada, throughout the Yukon, across the territories, the entire northern parts of the Prairies, northern Ontario, Quebec, and including the Atlantic provinces.
There is not a region in this country that is not affected by the mining industry. From downtown Toronto to the smallest and most isolated northern community the effect of the mining industry is felt either directly or indirectly. When one considers the tens of thousands of people employed by the mining industry, the billions of dollars of business activity generated on an annual basis from this industry, the tremendous amount of tax revenues that accrue to various levels of Government from the industry, as well as the tremendous trade benefits that accrue, for Canada this is a major industry, and of particular interest in the regions of Canada.
We all recognize that the economic prosperity that has occurred in pockets of southern Ontario has not necessarily occurred in other parts of Canada. I remember back in 1986 when the Government pointed out that 95 per cent of all jobs created that year were created within 100 miles of the CN Tower in downtown Toronto. This meant that for most of Canada no jobs were created in 1986 in terms of net gain. Whether it is the Yukon, the Prince Rupert area, across the Kootenay regions of British Columbia, the northern part of Manitoba, or the northern part of Ontario, we are talking about single industry towns and communities which depend either exclusively or largely on the mining industry.
We recognize that the mining industry is a cyclical industry which is vulnerable to the international market-place and, consequently, vulnerable to cyclical trends in the market. We know about the boom and bust situation which exists in the industry. The flow-through mechanism was a method whereby this benefit could be spread over the years so that a net financial gain was always accruing to areas which happened to be nearby or within mineralized zones of the country.
March 3, 1988

Earlier today I had an opportunity to speak with a number of brokers in Kamloops, representatives of the B.C. Mining Association, representatives of the local chamber of commerce, presidents of some exploration companies, as well as some prospectors themselves. These individuals brought home very clearly that the particular flow-through share mechanism was absolutely necessary if we hoped to maintain present levels of exploration in these areas, and particularly if we hoped to see any increase in these levels.
In my own constituency literally hundreds of people have been employed in the last few months. They were previously unemployed, but they are now out in the field staking claims, trenching, drilling, and carrying out all other activities associated with mining exploration, in the hopes of identifying an appropriate ore body and establishing a full mine one day.
When we talk about the benefits of the flow-through mechanism we have a number of supporters. It is not only the New Democratic Party which feels that this initiative must be maintained. I refer, for example, to the White Paper on tax reform, sponsored by the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. After analysing the particular program, the committee wrote a report, and I would like to refer to the section dealing with the flow-through share mechanism. I want to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the committee heard from mining associations, prospectors, developers, brokers, and corporations in the mining industry-a whole host of witnesses.
The committee indicated that a study done by the Association of Prospectors of Quebec found that the flow-through mechanism and related incentives for the mining sector contributed to the realization of 71 public share issues in 1985, of which 38 were from junior companies and 33 were from flow-through shares, and resulted in 25 discoveries that in future may generate profits, 66,000 jobs, $2.8 billion of value added, and $300 million of net income for federal and provincial Governments. This was simply one witness indicating what had happened in one part of Canada as a result of the flow-through mechanism.

speechtext: Who is opposing these flow-through shares?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
I do not know if you heard the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), Mr. Speaker, but he asks: "Who is opposing these flow-through shares?" Obviously the finance committee found that its witnesses thought that it was an excellent idea, and I will indicate in a moment others who thought that it was an excellent idea. As I look around the Chamber 1 can only assume, since we will be having a vote later, that it must be the Conservatives who oppose it. I know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) made clear in his presentation that he was against it, but I also know that there are members in the Conservative caucus-and I would like to think that it is the overwhelming majority-who actually believe in this principle. Whether they have the courage of
Supply
their conviction will be seen later this afternoon when we get to the vote.
Another group representing federal and provincial organizations formed a subcommittee on mineral taxation and gave a report to the Government in which it indicated that the junior mining sector in particular would be hurt by tax reform changes affecting flow-through shares. It feared that a reduction in exploration could lead to a serious decline in economic activity in remote regions. That joint federal-provincial group of organizations made clear in its recommendations that to tamper with the flow-through share mechanism would cause serious problems in the country.
We could also look to what the Mining Association of Canada had to say. For example, it indicated that large amounts of funds had been raised for exploration in Canada through the medium of flow-through equity share financing, and that the device had been particularly significant in giving access to capital to junior mining companies as distinct from senior or producing mining companies, although a number of senior companies not in a taxable position had also found the device useful. The individuals representing the Mining Association of Canada indicated clearly that the mechanism played a very, important role in their development.
The February 15 edition of the Northern Miner contained a very interesting article. It reminded us of the recently formed save flow-through committee representing tens of thousands of people involved in the mining industry across Canada, from Fabrador to Vancouver Island and up to the northern tips of the Yukon and the territories. Thousands and thousands of Canadians representing the mining industry have come together in a desperate move to try to bring the Government to its senses, to try to make it understand that if it continues with its plans to gut the flow-through share mechanism it will have a severely negative impact on these communities in Canada. They pointed out that in 1987 alone more than $900 million in flow-through money was raised to assist the mining communities and mining areas of Canada through exploration activity.
I do not have the time to refer to every area and to indicate why this particular tax provision was so important for the future of the areas they represent, virtually every major mining area of the country. I wish I had the time to do so because they pointed out the tens of thousands of new claims as a result of activities over the last few years and the hundreds of millions of dollars in new mines and new mining properties that have been developed. It is really tremendous.
I have looked at the briefs presented to Members of Parliament which point out that not only do the mining industry and the miners involved benefit directly. However, if we look at the Northern Miner magazine, we see pages and pages of related industries attached directly to the program.

In some areas, things may have improved marginally. I think of the kind of changes that have occurred in the Yukon. The territorial Government has taken a whole set of measures over the last number of months that have decreased employment substantially and encouraged a great deal of economic activity, particularly in the mining industry. The Government of the Yukon feels so seriously about this particular measure that-

As soon as Mr. Penikett in the Yukon heard that the Government had decided to destroy the effectiveness of the flow-through share tax provisions, he was in touch with the Minister of Finance pointing out what this would do to that particular part of the territories.
I wondered if the other representatives of the territories have bothered to mention this to the Minister of Finance. I have not heard them in debate today. As a matter of fact, I cannot recall ever hearing them raise this matter in the House of
Commons. The day is not over yet. Perhaps we will hear them speak in favour of this motion later.
In the regions, Canadians are doing their best in spite of the Government's actions to generate activity in their regions, to take initiative in local communities, and to take advantage of those few provisions in the tax system that give them some encouragement and support in their activities. In areas like the Kootenay region of British Columbia, this has been important. The people of those areas are mystified about why the Government seems to be cutting back.
I can say without any hesitation, on behalf of my colleagues from constituencies like Thunder Bay-Atikokan, Thunder Bay-Nipigon, Skeena, St. John's East, Prince Albert, Yukon, New Westminster-Coquitlam, Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands, Nickel Belt, Kenora-Rainy River and Churchill as well as many others, just to name a few, that we will be standing in our places, shoulder to shoulder, unanimously supporting the reintroduction of these flow-through shares. I will be watching carefully the representatives of the Territories to see how they will be voting, knowing that their constituents will be more than interested in whether or not they rise.
People from the Kootenays, the Lac-Saint-Jean region, the Okanagan Valley, Timiskaming, Timmins, Prince George, other parts of northern British Columbia, northern Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and of course Quebec will be watching. I suspect that tonight most Canadians will be riveted to their television sets when that vote takes place to see whether or not those who represent them rise.
I do not like embarrassing anyone, and I will not do so today, but I could have read into the record a whole number of letters to the editor sent by Conservative Members about their support for the flow-through share mechanism. Many of them feel that the decision to gut this program was not a good one and they would like to see it changed. In the spirit of cooperativeness and positiveness and in an attempt to make this a businesslike place, we would provide an opportunity for those Members to indicate how serious they are this afternoon, or are they simply writing about their interest as opposed to standing up, as a Member of Parliament ought to for his or her constituents?
This motion provides an opportunity for all Members of the House to speak. This is a non-partisan issue. This is one of those issues in which politics ought not play any role at all, quite frankly. When I look across the aisle at my Conservative friends, knowing how they feel about this issue-

Mr. Speaker, I simply cannot let that very able speech go by. My friend from Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) has put the case for a special deduction for a particular industry very well. I think he would agree that it is a very generous deduction, a deduction of 133 per cent. What he also knows but did not put very well was that all sorts of other sectors want these deductions as well. There is no doubt that if one can invest $1 and deduct $1.33 from one's tax, one is doing very well.
During the three election campaigns in which I have campaigned against the NDP, NDP Members have identified each time the tens of thousands of Canadians who have not had to pay income tax because of these special deductions, whether they be for the film industry or the oil industry. Is the Hon. Member now saying that members of the NDP will forever stop going after these 60,000 people who do not pay income tax because they take advantage of the special deductions? Is the Hon. Member prepared to back off on his attack on those people and say that he recognizes that they are making investments and that they therefore should not have to pay income tax?
The logical flow-through of that is that ordinary Canadians have to pay more if we let the top people take these special deductions and not pay their fair share. Is that what members of the NDP are saying?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is not quite what we are saying. I too recall the last federal election campaign. At that time, the issue was a minimum personal tax. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), as a matter of fact all three Leaders, said during that very famous debate that they felt that a minimum personal tax was appropriate.
Supply
Since we now have in place the mechanism for a minimum personal tax, and though there are still a few exceptions who somehow slip through the cracks, we feel that by and large everyone now pays at least a minimum tax. In terms of the personal tax system, there is some equity now in the system.
Those people who will provide the flow-through money by providing equity financing for resource companies will still be required to pay a minimum tax, even if they use significant tax reductions to bring their incomes down. We all agree with that minimum tax, I suppose, if we believe the Leaders of the various political Parties and their commitments to that and the legislation that was subsequently passed in the House.
I think the Hon. Member is referring to the 60,000 corporations that do not pay any income tax in spite of profits. He knows very well that the flow-through program accrues by and large to companies that are not in taxable positions. That is why the flow-through mechanism makes it through the company and into the hands of certain investors who will in fact pay a minimum tax.
We are talking about 60,000 profitable corporations. I use the word "profitable" because too often people are under the impression that we want to tax unprofitable companies. That does not make any sense. However, companies like Brascan, Cadillac-Fairview, the Royal Bank of Canada and Alcan have profits of perhaps S200 million or $300 million. We say that companies with profits like that should pay some income tax. The Mom and Pop shops next door, the small welding shop, all pay taxes if they are profitable. We are simply saying that should also apply to the large corporations and multinational branch plants. I think we agree on this, if I understand my friend's question correctly.

Mr. Speaker, I have a comment and a question for the Hon. Member. 1 know he has had a long interest in tax matters. Yet what we are witnessing today is something very remarkable. We are witnessing the greatest transformation in a political Party and the greatest flip-flop on policy we have ever seen. The NDP has decided to endorse tax benefits for the rich!
I am very familiar with flow-through shares. For three years prior to being elected I was with a mining company in Edmonton. It was listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange and it survived on flow-through shares. My salary came from flowthrough shares. It did not come from income from gold or silver mining, which we were ostensibly doing. It came from flow-through shares and from doctors, lawyers and dentists in Toronto. I know where the money came from. Yet the same people who pay the money and take the tax breaks are the ones that the NDP complain about.
Tax Probe, led by the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis), went around talking about fairness and how there are all these tax breaks for wealthy Canadians. The official critic in this area for the NDP, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), was talking about tax breaks recently. He said that when we are talking about tax savings, we are talking about someone else paying that amount. If that amount is not paid by the taxpayer, we are all going to be paying it, as we have been reminded by the Government many times. He said he did not think there were many people in his constituency in a position to sink $10,000 into oil, gas or mining exploration. He went on to say that he felt these benefits, flow-through shares and others, were strictly for the rich.
The Hon. Member will also know that his official critic, myself and some others were in New Zealand a week or two ago. That country has a Labour Government. For a Labour Government, it has been doing some strange things. It put in place a flat tax. There is no capital gains tax. It has been privatizing government departments. It also introduced a tax on food.

Everyone in Timiskaming, in all the communities of northern

Canada, and everyone in the mining sector knew then and knows today where the NDP stands. The NDP is not fooling anyone with this motion today. The NDP is still against flowthrough shares. This is nothing but politics being played here today.
On December 16, 1986, the Member for Ottawa Centre participated in a debate here on Bill C-23. As reported in Hansard at page 2171, he said:
-we should simply tell the Government to stop it, take the measure away, start all over again, and strike out the loopholes.
A September 26, 1987, editorial in one of the papers in my riding said:
The NDP are likely the spearhead of the effort that helped decimate the flow-through plan in the last Budget.

It is Tuesday before we hear anything from them about flow-through shares.
What has the Government and the Minister of Finance done? A proposal for the alteration of the flow-through shares investment mechanism was suggested by the Government with its introduction of tax reform. As a result of the proposals in this comprehensive package, finance officials and Government Members consulted with the mining industry to find out the future effect of the proposed changes.
In December, the Minister of Finance announced the changes to his proposals. The mining industry continues to have concerns, so the Government has undertaken to consult further with representatives of the mining industry and with interested groups and individuals across the country on the impact of the changes. Meetings have taken place this week and will continue with individuals across the country.
In the past few months much progress has been made. The button I am wearing today is from the flow-through committee of Kirkland Lake, including Evelyn Kasner, Rene Adams,
March 3, 1988

Mayor Joe Mavrinac, and other individuals from our community, who along with prospectors and developers from the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and chambers of commerce across the country have been meeting, i and members of my caucus from coast to coast have been meeting with them and with individuals from the investment community. We will be working with them to see what can be done.
It should be pointed out that flow-through shares are not gone, as some Members would like to suggest. On December 16, the Minister announced as part of the Notice of Ways and Means Motion adjustments to the June 18 proposals that pertain to flow-through shares. These include a slower phaseout of earned depletion. Therefore, the depletion rates will be as follows: 33-1/3 per cent until June 30, 1988; 16-2/3 per cent from July 1, 1988, to February 28, 1990, which is extended from June 30, 1989, as had been proposed in the June 18 White Paper.
Earned depletion will be excluded from the CNIL pool and only 50 per cent of Canadian exploration expense will be included in the pool. The additional eight-month extension of depletion will facilitate the adjustment process of the exploration sector to the new rules. The adjustment to the CNIL rules will improve the attractiveness of flow-through shares to many investors who would otherwise have been discouraged from investing in them under the June 18 proposals.
The Minister of Finance also announced that the federal Government will continue to monitor mineral exploration levels in the future, and will introduce appropriate measures, if and when they are needed for exploration and regional development.
Over-all, the change to the CNIL rules and to depletion have the purpose of providing an incentive level high enough to ensure adequate levels of investment in flow-through shares. However, let us also remember that on October 19, the stock market crashed. No one could control the stock market, and the investment funds that would be flowing into flow-through shares completely dried up. Anyone involved in the investment community will say that the financing that was available in June and September, 1987, is not there today because it was lost on the market.
When one considers this additional problem, returning flowthrough shares to 133 per cent may not be the answer. The Minister of Finance wants to consult with those involved in the mining and investment communities to ensure that if adjustments will be considered the proper adjustments are made. It is a simple matter to put the flow-through shares back to 133 per cent, but what happens in six weeks or six months if the investment climate has not changed? Will they admit they were wrong and ask the Minister to make another adjustment?

I was sent here to work for my constituents, for the betterment of the mining community and the betterment of all Canadians. I am not here to spend a day in the House to respond to a Party that suddenly recognizes that there is a mining community, with a Member who until today and yesterday did not realize there was a future in mining. They knew nothing about mining. I can put on the record today that the mining community is not new to me. I will be speaking for the mining community in northern Ontario and across this country for many years to come. I regret to see what has gone on here today. Let me say that I will vote with my Government because we have the answers for the future. We are working on the problems of flow-through shares and we will ensure the future of our communities and the mining sector for many years to come.

I am glad to have a chance to speak to the amendment, moved by the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), to the motion of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy). The amendment spells out in clear detail that we are not just talking about flow-through shares here but about the earned depletion allowance. Every time that I or other Members have put a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) asking him to reinstate the earned depletion allowance, he slides off on the limp excuse that we have flow-through shares. We know that we have flow-through shares. That is not the problem.
The problem is that the Government is phasing out the earned depletion allowance. The motion of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre does not spell out the 33 per cent earned depletion allowance which is the crux of the problem facing hundreds of communities across the country with the collapse of the stock market last October and the loss of equity investments. Added to that general problem in the market, especially in junior mines, is the loss of the earned depletion allowance that has been in place since 1982. It has been very successful in creating employment in communities throughout northern Ontario, northern Quebec and many other parts of the country.
The magnitude of the economic activity in those communities could not have been generated in any other way. Every mining community eventually faces the problem of diversification or renewal with new mines. It often happens that new ore bodies are found. Some 10 years ago Timmins was in a very bad way. It is now a booming and prospering community with many new mining activities. Similarly, the Kirkland Lake area was suffering from the lack of new ore bodies.
The Minister and his officials in the Department of Finance argue that this may not be as efficient a way to create economic activity in those mining communities as some other method. What that overlooks is the tremendous social investment that we have in these communities. Hundreds of millions of dollars have been invested in housing, streets, schools, churches, commercial enterprises and so on. There are not many instruments that the federal Government has. The provincial Governments have many more which perhaps deliver the type of payload in terms of economic activity.
In this respect I need only look at the area around Wawa and the mining operations that are opening up there. We faced the problem with the iron steel industry of Algoma Steel cutting back its economic activity by several hundred jobs at the Wawa mines. We now see tremendous mineral exploration and development activity moving down from the Hemlo field into the Wawa area to Batchawana, where there is a great deal of activity.
A couple of years ago we faced the prospect of the possible shutdown of Wawa. The ability to diversify that economy and
Supply
bring in some other means of economic activity were very limited. I attended meetings with respect to what activities could take place there, even though it is not in my constituency. Tourism or a specialized pulp and paper operation and so on were considered. Fortunately, the generation of hundreds of millions of dollars that we have seen through the earned depletion allowance in flow-through shares has made possible important discoveries there. Thus the social costs which have been paid in that community will be used. People will be living there. They will have new jobs in new mining activities.
The earned depletion allowance is used for the most risky part of mining exploration and development. Flow-through shares will do the job once one gets to the development of the mine itself. But at the exploration stage money is needed, with a tremendous incentive. That is why we have a 33 per cent incentive on top of the 100 per cent write-off for those people who want to invest. In Quebec there is a 166 per cent incentive because the province, up to the limits of its income tax system, provides an additional incentive.
We are not only looking at exploration and development activity since in a way it is only the catalyst. Even though we are talking about $400 million or $500 million per year being generated for exploration development, those are small amounts of money compared to what is seen once the ore body is delineated and development starts and contracts are let for sales overseas. I take the example of Elliot Lake and the development of the mines at Denison and Rio Algom which were developed back in the early 1960s. They involved some $300 million in the one case and $400 million in the other just to develop two or three existing mines to put them into modern operations.
If we want to have mines actually being developed three, four, or five years down the road, since these things do not happen over night, then we have to make the commitment of funds now for exploration and development. This is why there has been such a tremendous outpouring and rallying this week at the symposium being held here on flow-through shares and earned depletion allowance at the Renaissance Hotel. Literally hundreds of people across the country who are concerned with economic development in the slow growth regions were here to protest the Government cutting off this program during the next 18 or 24 months. They are here to demand that the Government follow through.
One of the officials there, Mr. Massicotte, who is a councillor in the Elliot Lake town council, is also the president of the Mining Municipalities of Ontario. There were a great many representatives from the Rouyn-Noranda area as well. They pointed out that between 1982 and 1986 the unemployment rate in that area due to intensive mining exploration development activity has fallen from some 26 per cent to 6 per cent. That is nothing short of a miracle. Every mining activity in the country is going through a contraction of employment compared to production of mineral because it has to be more

efficient, more automated and more safety related. To see the unemployment rate drop in an area which has been mined for several generations now due to the flow-through share and the earned depletion allowance is nothing short of a miracle.
However, there is another aspect to this. Although most of the resource areas are relatively active, prosperous, and unemployment is down, much of that prosperity has taken place in the last 12 months. The employment was there, but the value of minerals, for example, copper and nickel have skyrocketed in the last 12 months. During the first several years after the recession from 1982 until the latter part of 1986 or early 1987, things were not that great, but with the mineral value going up, the economies are blossoming in places such as Sudbury, Hemlo, Wawa, and the Kirkland Lake area. I talked to a mining exploration development engineer who was doing a lot of work in my constituency in Batchawana, an area along the Lake Superior shore about 50 miles north of Sault Ste. Marie. He stated that they did not know, but they thought that there were five mineral deposits there that may turn out to be of production quality, but whether funds can be generated to carry out the detailed analysis and development is all dependent on this whole system.
1 cannot understand why the Minister of Finance when asked if he would reinstate earned depletion allowance and retain the flow-through shares stated: "The problem is that the equity markets all collapsed with the stock market crash last October 19". We agree that that is one of the problems. But with the equity markets down, the interest down, now is the time to maintain this mechanism for generating hundreds of millions of dollars, some $300 million in Ontario last year, and I understand from an earlier figure back in the early 1980s of only $100 million.

It would be easy to list every municipality that is concerned about this matter. I would like to read a letter from Mayor Thomas Despres, who lives in the constituency of the Hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall). In the letter Mayor Despres spells out how important this is. How the Hon. Member for Timiskaming can vote against the motion, I am not clear. Since the economy of Haileybury and Northern Ontario have grown dependent upon the activities of mining and exploration, it is my feeling that "flow-through" investments have been, and hopefully will continue to be, a major stimulant to both the community of Northern Ontario and Canada as a whole. However, I believe the announced tax reform will retard our economic
progress and leave ourselves vulnerable to economic instability. This can and will result in loss of jobs in areas that have been traditionally economically disadvantaged.
Therefore, will you please-urge Mr. Wilson and the Finance Committee to re-evaluate the effects of tax reform on "flow-through" investments. The livelihood of many northerners is at stake.
That letter was signed by the Mayor of Haileybury. I have similar letters from the Town of Elliot Lake, the Township of Michipicoten, which is the community of Wawa, which call on the Government to reinstate this program because it is essential.
The last point I wish to make is terribly important. A report was given in the last issue of the international mining magazine, The Journal of Mining, which tends to indicate that the reason the earned depletion allowance is being phased out is due to the free trade deal between Canada and the United States. That is very disturbing.
The Americans have different ways of doing regional development. They build military bases, and there are hundreds of them across the states. They have procurement programs, and so on. We have a distinctive way of providing regional development, and I think that we do a better job.
Last week I was in Fredericton with the Liberal caucus task force on free trade. A representative of McCain Foods described the impact that free trade would have on the operations of that company and on the Province of New Brunswick. Someone put forward the argument that the New England states, for example Maine, have a similar land base to New Brunswick and they have had free trade with the rest of the states for years. There is not a poultry operation, egg laying operation, very little dairy or food processing, yet they have the same land mass as provinces like New Brunswick which has a very well developed food processing industry with companies like McCain, and a reasonably prosperous dairy industry. Our system of regional development is our own. But with this deal that is proposed we will not have the freedom.
In an editorial in the Mining Journal of February 5, 1988, published in London, Mr. Karl Glackmeyer, Director of the Prospectors and Developers Association told the mining magazine that the proposed reduction in the earned depletion allowance will effectively eliminate flow-through funding and could put 10,000 jobs in northern Quebec at risk, and will threaten new mining projects. Ottawa's position is that the incentives have to be eliminated in accordance with the recently agreed Canada-U.S. free trade agreement. Mr. Glackmeyer suggests that the reduction be gradually phased out over a decade rather than being cut off over 12 months.
I do not think it is should be phased out at all. Our finance critic has suggested that we commit ourselves for a five-year period, and at that time it is reviewed to see if it is still necessary and useful. The article further points out that $900 million was spent in mining exploration in Canada during the last year.
March 3, 1988

That is one side of the coin of the free trade deal as it affects the earned depletion allowance. The second part of the equation, which was pointed out in an article by a financial accounting house in Toronto, is that once it is phased out it will not be possible to reinstitute it in Canada as an incentive for regional development for mining exploration and development without Canada being subject to countervail or other attacks of remedial action by the United States.
That is very serious business. This responsible mining journal states that this tax mechanism that has generated $400 million or $500 million is being phased out because of the trade deal. We are puzzled about why the Government is doing it and what will be the long-term implications. Surely they will not be good ones. Also, we are surprised that the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Centre came on side and supported flow-through shares. A couple of years ago the Hon. Member clearly indicated that he was not in favour of earned depletion allowance. The issue is important in my part of the country in terms of employment and in terms of providing funds for an industry involved in an extremely risky business. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to have the opportunity to speak on my Party's motion concerning flow-through shares. It is necessary for Canada's prosperity and economy to continue the arrangements which have produced such impressive results in the mining exploration industry and which have had dramatic, positive repercussions not only across northern Canada but also in some of the major economic centres.
I am glad to say that we have before us a motion which is quite specific and is not phrased in partisan terms or indeed in terms that anyone in the House could find offensive either to conscience or political position. Instead, it is a motion that is substantive, meaningful and addresses an issue of great importance and significance, particularly to the remote areas of Canada, the resource communities, many of which are like the ones I have the privilege of representing in this House.
The motion reads:
That this House notes that the flow-through share tax provision has been
instrumental in revitalizing mining communities and regions across Canada,
and consequently urges that the initial benefit level of this provision not be
reduced but be retained-
No one would argue with the proposition, particularly in so far as precious metal deposits are concerned, that the flowthrough share tax provision has indeed been instrumental in revitalizing communities. The total value of investment by means of the flow-through share mechanism, since it was brought in in 1983, has been in the order of $2 billion. That investment has gone largely to communities which, prior to 1983, were depressed, some to very considerable degrees, not having the exploration and mining development business on which they had grown and prospered in the past.
The interest-rate crisis under the Liberal Government of 1981-82 had largely eliminated the pool of capital which had been flowing previously into mining developments, most of it of a speculative or risky nature. The high interest rate policy pursued by the Liberal Government had soaked up capital, drawing it into short-term instruments and mere financial instruments such as bonds, guaranteed income certificates and term deposits. It had taken away the pool of funds which had previously gone into investments that led to the development of Canadian communities, particularly in resource areas.
Unlike many other corporate tax measures, the flow-through share provisions have extended benefits almost uniformly across northern Canada and, by the interchange of expenditures and the sourcing of materials, services and personnel, right through into major economic headquarters such as Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal. These are the places where
March 3, 1988

many of the most profitable parts of the exercise such as financing are in fact carried out. This measure was not one of those corporate tax measures which simply gave funds to those large companies which were already prosperous and left with them funds that could have been recaptured for financing social services, economic development expenditures and regional equalization. By contrast with those sorts of measures, the flow-through tax share provisions spread benefits throughout the economy from community to community across northern Canada.
Because of the well-known multiplier effect which of course is much more significant outside small communities, indeed this measure spread those benefits right through the Canadian economy. Most tax expenditures go to the major centres of corporate activity. They go particularly to Toronto and the Golden Horseshoe. By contrast, this specific tax measure spread benefits right through the economy.
Prior to 1983, the rate of development of new mines in Canada was at a level of about 4 per cent, comparing new mine development with the productivity of existing mines. In the five years or so since this flow-through provision has been in effect, that rate has quadrupled so that we now have, primarily in the precious metals sector, a level of new mine development in the order of 16 per cent.
Over those five years, approximately 60 new exploration and development properties have been started by flow-through share investment, some in locations such as Nova Scotia where there had always been the potential but no development. In 1987 alone, about 35 new mines were opened, most of them small, it is true, most of them not Mom and Pop operations but on the level of 50 or 100 employees. These 35 mines have provided employment in communities across Canada which prior to the coming on stream of these mines had indeed been economically depressed.
The operation of flow-through shares produced regional development without favouritism, without patronage and without political partiality. In truth, it produced economic development in an equitable and democratic fashion. That is indeed the sort of economic development that I and my Party want to see, the kind we will be encouraging and promoting when we form the Government of this country.
That regional development was truly benefiting all the regions of Canada which had previously been economically depressed. There were some exceptions where there was not adequate mineralization to permit profitable exploration.
For those Members of the House who do not represent mining communities and are not familiar with the dynamics of exploration and development, it bears pointing out that most of the actual work in exploration and development is done by junior resource companies and sometimes still by individual prospectors. In many cases, small consortia of individual
Supply
investors group into what are known as junior mining companies. In many cases, the people involved live in the communities which are close to where the exploration is being done. Of course, some of the more highly trained geological and geomorphological consultants operate out of major communities with excellent transportation networks. Yet we see a high degree of turnover of these funds within the mining community.
I noticed that in the past the Mayor of Kirkland Lake referred to large exploration companies as robber barons. Without being too harsh on that judgment, I would say that if there were improvements that could be made in the flowthrough share structure, we in the NDP would seek improvements to increase the percentage of funds generated by the shares to the small and medium-sized exploration companies, the individual junior listings, rather than the major companies and major consortia. The economic development brought by smaller companies is more equitable and more widespread. It represents a better spreading through the economy of that multiplier effect. The profits, when they are made, are generally spent or invested in these or neighbouring communities rather than being repatriated to a major corporate headquarters.
We know that the tax value of flow-through shares has been cut in half, according to the White Paper tax changes. The Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs asked that the depletion allowance be continued to keep the value of shares at the present level, and it bears pointing out that that is an all-Party committee of this House.
In addition to investment in exploration and development, flow-through shares indirectly encourage, over time, more processing in the communities where the mining takes place. Prior to the introduction of flow-through shares, mining communities were experiencing cyclical busts and booms, like any other resource economy, with some communities becoming ghost towns within months. We do not expect that the continuation of flow-through shares is going to lead to elimination of that cycle in resource economies, mining in particular. We know there will always be ups and downs.
As northerners we realize that every boom in mining exploration is going to produce a drop-off period in which there is consolidation, analysis, a period in which financing must be arranged and in which strategic decisions must be made vis-a-vis the development of one property or another. However, we do know we have experienced very popular results in economic terms in the vast majority of those communities where flow-through shares have had an impact on resource development.
I would like to address a point which I think is worthy of note by all Members of this House. Mining communities very

March 3, 1988
Supply
often have extremely expensive social capital and infrastructure. Obviously they are built in areas of significant mineralization and the very minerals being sought are geologically bound and integrated with the Canadian Shield. I note, for example, that in the community of Red Lake in my riding it costs twice as much to service a single house with sewers and water as it does in the community of Dryden, some 160 kilometres to the south in an agricultural clay belt area where soils are far easier to penetrate. What that means when we have these high levels of investment in social capital is that there has to be a productive economy creating wealth, paying salaries higher than the Canadian average, if people are to enjoy a standard of living on a level with the average across this country. Mining communities, traditionally and almost without exception, face these higher costs and require that steady stream of new development work to produce the wealth capable of providing those services.
Let us also not forget the degree to which mining profits and mining income benefit the exchequers of this country, both provincially and federally. Let us not forget that people are out there even now as I speak drilling in the bush. It is 10, 15 or 20 degrees below zero and they are running drills. They are running drills in the Yukon, around Red Lake, Kirkland Lake and Val d'Or. They are well paid, as they should be, and because of that they are producing very significant returns to government exchequers.
The history of mineral development in this country has of course been cyclical, as indeed it is in almost all other countries. There have been some unattractive phases to it. We had the gold rush with a terrible toll in lives and health. We had the period when financing was virtually unregulated and fortunes were made and lost, largely lost, by means of the operation of unethical financing instruments and unethical financiers. Yet the mineral resource development industry is part and parcel, indeed a keystone, of the varied economic development of Canada.
There is, I believe, a fundamental interest for all Canadians, even in the larger centres, that there be healthy economies in remote communities. With those healthy economies we ensure that remote communities do not become ghost towns and people do not have to move everything and lose all the equity they built up in the community; not only the equity in their homes but all they have contributed to the development of a community. That is the sort of economic development that my Party is seeking and wishes to further in consideration of the extension of these flow-through provisions.
It has been said, and I have not heard the observation refuted yet, that one of the reasons for eliminating flowthrough shares is because it will be found to be a subsidy under the trade agreement the Government signed with the United States. I believe that is not a good reason for eliminating a successful financing provision. It should be a good reason for negotiating again with the U.S. concerning its acceptability, and ensuring that there is some acceptance. As the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) observed earlier, the U.S. does its regional development, bearing in mind its task is much less than in Canada because of the size of the economy and the
smallness of their geography, in very different ways which sometimes have more of a private sector flavour, a more capitalist bent. These include financing military research and distribution of military facilities, which are very powerful regional development instruments nonetheless.
We should look very carefully, and the Government should study this if it has not already done so, at the effectiveness of flow-through shares as a tax creator. As I said, through the multiplier effect I believe it is possible to demonstrate that, unlike the scientific investment research tax credit introduced by the last Government and which ended up costing an enormous amount, some of which was used to finance research in Brazil, we could prove that the flow-through share mechanism has produced an over-all positive cash flow to the federal and provincial Treasuries.
As my Party's spokesman on mines, I had the opportunity on several occasions to bring attention to this mechanism in this House. I note that in my statement of Wednesday, December 9, I quoted the Leader of my Party who was addressing I'association canadienne des prospecteurs et entrepreneurs of Rouyn-Noranda when he said this fiscal measure corresponds well to the objectives of our Party with respect to the creation of jobs and development of resource-based regions. I am very pleased to be able to put that on the record again today.
Let us look at financing for a moment. As the Prospectors and Developers Association of Canada says, many junior companies which rely exclusively on equity financing will be forced out of the market. It is of course easy for people to make judgments on the proliferation of junior mining companies. Yet what it does show is that the participation in the mining industry of this country is being democratized. My Party would like to see it further democratized by making it possible for smaller initial investments to purchase flowthrough shares than has been the case up until now.
Within my riding I have seen some very profound benefits from flow-through shares. There are three areas in particular; the Red Lake gold area which has historically been the second largest producing area in Canada, the Pickle Lake area, and the area around Cameron Lake south of Kenora. I had the opportunity to meet with the mining recorder in Red Lake some three weeks ago and I was amazed by what I saw and heard.
His office was jammed to the rafters with charts, maps and geological analyses. He told me of the ripple effect right through the economy in that community. The reeve has estimated that it has affected approximately 25 per cent of the total economic activity in the community. It has affected the hospitality industry, the supply industry, the maintenance of mining equipment, and the furbishing of provisions right down to a shelter workshop which is doing a booming business making core trays for storing the mining cores. The effects are going right through the community to the point where there are now approximately 26 drills currently operating in Red Lake whereas five years ago there were three.
March 3, 1988

Similarly, the community of Pickle Lake, which had been gravely depressed by the pull-out of the Umex mine, is now again enjoying a very healthy economy because of the number of drills that are running in locations around Pickle Lake. Also, partly as a result of flow-through shares, there are three properties in the Kenora area which are very close to coming on stream.
Let us look at this motion realistically. This motion is not partisan. It is simply supportive of something which has proven successful in economic development. I believe that every Member of this House could and indeed should support this motion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this important debate on the tax principles of this Government and this country. But it is also very important to show the hyprocrisy of our colleagues opposite, the Members of the New Democratic Party.
The proposal made in the White Paper on tax reform which was amended in December and then tabled does not in any way eliminate tax incentives for the mining industry; indeed the tax provisions specifically designed for the mining sector remain unchanged. Percentages vary at some levels, and this is important; from 133 they drop down to 100 and this reflects the over-all approach of the tax reform. Thanks to tax reform, nine Canadians out of ten will pay less income tax, and nine elderly Canadians out of ten will either pay less income tax or none at all. We should keep that in mind when we look at the tax reform proposals. We can't pick what suits us and throw out the rest.
I think the Minister of Finance and the Conservative Government have shown that they know how to manage and administer this country. We reduced the deficit, and we managed to introduce proposals for a fairer and more equitable tax system. Once again, Mr. Speaker, tax reform provides for changes in various sectors. The mining industry, like all other small businesses, will see a reduction in its income tax rate. I did not hear anyone mention this particular point today, but it is an important one. The tax rate for mining companies will go down, and that applies to both junior companies and companies with annual profits of over $200,000.
Flow-through shares will be maintained, and they will help mining companies pass on unused tax incentives to their investors. I think we ought to be realistic and be aware of what the situation actually is like.

March 3, 1988

Mr. Speaker, we have talked about regional development practically all day. That is exactly why we have tax reform. The main purpose is to have an Income Tax Act that collects revenue, although I am sure, Mr. Speaker, you do not really like the idea and in fact not many people do. The purpose of the Income Tax Act, however, is not to provide for regional, cultural or social development. The purpose of the Income Tax Act is to collect revenue and hand it over to the departments concerned: Employment and Immigration, Energy, Mines and Resources, DRIE, and so forth. The Departments, which have people who are qualified and who know their business, can then distribute this money in the proper fashion.
Mr. Speaker, I hope Opposition Members don't want to go back to the scientific research tax credit scheme which cost Canadians billions but never did those who needed it any good. Our scientists never got anything out of it. They never got a cent.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and my colleague from Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce) pointed out to me that the then Minister of Finance in that red period-worse than a black period, it was a red period-knew about it but did nothing, and those billions of dollars slipped into the hands of most everybody except those who should have got them. This must be stopped. This is what tax reform is all about.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) emphasized this, the Minister of Finance emphasized it, and I think that on this side of the House we all agreed with that if in the future this Government were to develop for the mining sector or for any other sector, a plan for Western development, a plan for Eastern Canada, Northern Ontario, Quebec. If the mining industry needs special help in line with the policies of the relevant Department, at that point there is nothing to prevent supporting the development of resources, Mr. Speaker. There is absolutely nothing to prevent that. There is not a single act that prevents that.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, flow-through shares as we know have done a lot for mining areas. They also to a degree created a supermarket. The investment rate was too high. Everyone who is familiar with that industry agrees that we cannot sustain the rate we had in 1986 and 1987 particularly. That rate cannot be sustained.
Therefore, the fact that the rate has gone from 133 per cent to 100 per cent does not mean the mining industry can no longer grow.
It does not mean either, Mr. Speaker, that this reduction that is in line with the spirit and the framework of the tax reform under which corporate and individual tax rates are going down, that does not mean that this Conservative Government, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) do not support regional development.
