This Government, Mr. Speaker, invested more into regional development than the previous Government over a comparable period of time. We have been doing profitable investment, Mr. Speaker.
When we refer to regional development, what does that imply? It implies helping businesses outside major centres.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that Trois-Rivieres is not what could be termed a major centre in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, in the constituency of Trois-Rivieres investments have created nearly 3,000 new jobs since 1984. That is regional development! And the same thing has been done across the land, in every industry and every region.
Mr. Speaker, let them not suggest that flow-through shares equal regional development. There is a Department of Regional Development, there is a Department to look after mines, there is another to look after tax laws; let each one do its job! But let people not think that the Income Tax Act is there to do everything because all that would be left to do would be to discard the 39 other Departments while keeping the Department of Finance, with 39 Ministers of State for Mines, Regional Development, this or that. I think we must be realistic.
Mr. Speaker, allow me also, and I think it is essential to point it out, to refer to the New Democratic Party and its position on flow-through shares.
On February 26, 1986, the Conservative Government introduced measures to improve flow-through shares. In September, 1986, the inquiry on the tax system carried out by the NDP indicated that the tax system is an ineffective tool to promote regional development.
Mr. Speaker, for once in 1986, the NDP agreed with a position taken by this Party and pursued by this Government since its election.
On December 12, the NDP voted against the measures in committee. On December 16, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) which we had the pleasure to hear today asked for the elimination of flow-through shares in this House. That was on December 16, 1986, less than two years ago, in fact some fourteen months ago. Some 14 months ago, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre who introduced a motion today asked in this House that flow-through shares be eliminated. And this is not all, Mr. Speaker.
On February 14, 1987, about a year ago, the NDP leader criticized flow-through shares saying that they were a mechanism through which the rich avoided to pay taxes. That was on February 14, 1987.
Mr. Speaker, you know that on behalf of the NDP leader, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre gives frigates to Quebec when he is in Quebec and gives them to New Brunswick when he is over there. Mr. Speaker, we would not have enough frigates with the NDP! They would need some in every province because they distribute them all over the place. The

On February 16, 1987, the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) stated that flow-through shares should be replaced by another program outside the tax system. In 1987, they agreed with us. However, the Hon. Member went further than we did. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my conviction that when this particular tax incentive was first introduced during the last Liberal administration, I doubt very much whether the then Minister of Finance really had a full realization of just how successful this measure would become as a tool of regional economic development. I think most Members in the House will know that if one did a comprehensive history of regional development policies in the country, one would discover that none of them have been particularly successful. It is not an area in which any Government has a particularly enviable or strong record.
There have been all sorts of experiments. There have been all sorts of endeavours. On occasion, large sums of money have been directed toward regional development policies and programs. But we know that none of them have worked particularly well. When Mr. Lalonde brought in this tax incentive, I do not think for a moment that he realized that here was a major tool of regional economic development and that we were going to go a long way in solving the problems in the remote resource-rich regions of the country.
That is what has happened. It has become a major tool of regional economic development. It began modestly. But, today, in remote resource-rich regions of Canada such as northern Ontario, northern Quebec, Newfoundland, north of 60 and in the northern parts of the other provinces, it really is the only thing standing between economic depression or something close to it and a relative degree of economic activity and some prosperity.
For example, when we look at the statistics for Ontario, we see that unemployment is down and growth is up. I was at Mr. Peterson's dinner on Tuesday evening. He is taking full credit for all the activity that is going on in Ontario. I do not remember him mentioning at all that the federal Government had much to do with it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION

Because it is the truth.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-FLOW-THROUGH SHARE TAX PROVISION
speechtext:
It is the truth that the federal Government has contributed next to nothing to the prosperity of Ontario. But certainly the federal Government has done not much at all in the North where the rates of unemployment are considerably higher than they are throughout Ontario generally.
The point I am making is that northern Ontario is not participating in the over-all prosperity of the province. Our rates of unemployment are well above the national average. We are having serious difficulty in maintaining our population and enjoying the prosperity that the other citizens of the province enjoy.
The one thing that we do have going for us is a great deal of activity in the mineral exploration business. It is evidenced if one goes to the City of Timmins. It can be seen in smaller communities such as Longlac and Geraldton. Throughout the North one can name any number of communities in this regard. There is some economic activity being generated. The question is: Why is the mineral exploration business so active? Why is it contributing in such an unbalanced and significant way to the economy of the resource-rich regions? The answer is simple and straightforward. The answer is that the flowthrough shares joined with the mining earned depletion allowance is what is having that effect.
A Sudbury chartered accountant calls this tax incentive, this flow through, the great unknown economic program. Austin Davey, the gentleman in question, is quoted in a journal called Northern Ontario Business as having said:
The tip of the iceberg is the tax incentive, the rest of the iceberg is jobs and
economic diversification in northern Canada.
In 1987 $1.1 billion was raised as a result of this tax incentive through the flow-through shares. Because mining exploration is labour intensive and because the mines are found in the North, the mechanism of flow-through shares is employing thousands of people in regions such as northern Ontario and the other ones I mentioned earlier.
I am participating in this debate simply to urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in the strongest terms that I can find: "Please, do not destroy a tax incentive which is contributing so much to regional development".
The money available for exploration through the flowthrough shares goes specifically to small and junior resource companies. That money is going to disappear entirely when this tax advantage becomes no more advantageous to the company in question or to the purchaser of the share than does buying an RRSP.
The Minister of Finance knows that it is not the big mining companies which are applying the pressure to preserve this investment scheme. Without flow-throughs the senior companies will be able to dominate the scene. They will be able to decide when exploration will take place. That will depend entirely on what is the world price of the mineral. If the world price goes up then there is exploration activity from the seniors. If the price goes down then the seniors become inactive and tend to put their money into other areas.

March 3, 1988
Supply
Once again, if we do not have the flow through and the mining earned depletion allowance, we are going to be back again into the boom and the bust cycle. That is something that we have been trying to avoid over the years with a variety of experiments in regional development.
This morning the Minister of Finance argued that it was not his tax reform policy that was the reason for the decline in investment for mining exploration. It is on the decline. He said, "Well, do not blame me. It is the state of mind of investors that has been caused by the stock market crash of last year". The Minister stated, "Investors are shy about buying equity, especially in areas like mining where the risk is high". I wish to tell the Minister of Finance that he has it all wrong. It is precisely because of the current attitude to the stock market that we need the full advantage of the flowthroughs. Flow-throughs become much less attractive if we do not have the 33 per cent mining earned depletion allowance. If we do not have that then junior stocks, which are among the highest risk investment in the stock exchanges, become totally unappealing to the investor. The advantage is needed to a greater extent today rather than when the market is buoyant. It is today we need it, and the Minister's explanation is very misleading.
To support this argument, I wish to refer to Mr. John Farche, President of the Prospectors and Developers Association, who makes the following statement in support of the view that I have just presented. He states:
At present, flow-through is the only viable means of raising-capital for exploration. Neither of the normal alternative financing sources will provide the funds we need.
Equity financing is crippled under present market conditions. And, in their current profit and cash positions, major companies will not have enough funds to keep up the momentum on exploration.
He further states:
Close to $33 million were raised after the October crash for expenditure before the MEDA phase-down in July. This confirms the fact that flowthroughs can perform, despite the market conditions, and that they are being crippled by the impending tax reform measures.
To emphasize and underline the point, I understand why the Minister of Finance would say, "Don't blame me. Look somewhere else", but he is wrong. It is not the state of mind toward the stock market at present which is causing a decline in investment in mining exploration, it is because of the tax reform proposal which will do away with the 33 per cent MEDA.
For resource regions of this country the full tax advantage of flow-throughs is just as important as is the Auto Pact to the industrial regions of the country. It is just as important as the
Auto Pact is to southern Ontario and to the automobile plants in the Province of Quebec.
I wish the House to know that, because of the flow-through shares, because of the mining earned depletion allowance, exploration activity in Canada has increased dramatically. There has been a 222 per cent increase in footage of diamond drilling in the last five years. Exploration efforts, largely due to the flow-through share financing, have brought about 34 new mines which are now committed to come on stream in 1987 and 1988. That is five times the typical average number of new projects, if that is taken over a period of time of the last 35 years. In addition, another 58 projects for future production are due to come forward as a result of the flow-through shares.
My hon. colleague, the Hon. Member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) referred to another area, quite apart from mining, and this is a hydro project in my constituency at Yellow Falls on the Matagami River. The site location was approved by the Ministry of National Resources, a pre-feasibility study funded by the Ontario Ministry of Energy was completed, and the project was considered feasible. It is estimated that this small project in my constituency where jobs are desperately needed will create 50 man-years of employment to complete the project. The barrier which recently appeared was the new federal Budget which eliminated rapid depreciation or flow through and it could render the Yellow Falls project unfeasible.
I have many more arguments to advance, Mr. Speaker. I will conclude by saying to the Minister of Finance: "You are a reasonable man. You know the reality of the resource regions. Please reconsider, and do not spoil a tool for regional development which is as important as it has become".
